Second, unleashing AI across the economy: accelerating AI adoption in key sectors including healthcare, education, energy, finance and public services, with specific recommendations for NHS AI deployment, an AI for Science Strategy, and the expansion of BridgeAI's regional adoption hubs. Third, securing the UK's future in AI: ensuring the UK benefits economically and secures domestic capability in frontier AI development, including through investment in UKRI's AI research programme and partnerships with leading AI laboratories. The Plan also includes a specific chapter on international AI leadership and positions the UK as a bridging actor between the US and EU approaches to AI governance.

items.title: 7th Basic Plan for the Promotion of Science and Technology
items.original_name: 第6期科学技術・イノベーション基本計画
items.org: Council for Science, Technology and Innovation (CSTI) / Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT) / Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI)
items.category: National – Strategy
items.document_name: 第6期科学技術・イノベーション基本計画
items.body:
Japan's national strategic framework for science, technology and innovation, covering the period FY2026–FY2030, which succeeds the 6th Basic Plan. Where the 6th Plan emphasised Society 5.0 as a social vision, the 7th Plan introduces an "actionable science" philosophy and places greater weight on three axes: revitalisation of Japan's basic research capabilities, acceleration of innovation-driven economic growth and integration of science and technology policy with economic security objectives.

The 7th Basic Plan was developed through a consultative process launched by Cabinet Office referral to the Council for Science, Technology and Innovation (CSTI) in December 2024, with a dedicated Expert Committee leading drafting through 2025 and a Cabinet decision adopted in March 2026. The Plan is structured around three strategic pillars. First, reviving Japan's research power: recognising a decade of declining research competitiveness, the Plan prioritises reform of the research environment through increased KAKENHI grants, postdoctoral support and university management reform. Second, innovation and industrial competitiveness: AI, semiconductors, quantum technologies, fusion energy, robotics and biotechnology are identified as strategic technology areas requiring end-to-end support from basic research through to social implementation. AI for Science is a prominent cross-cutting theme, covering AI-enabled research data infrastructure, autonomous laboratory systems and AI integration into research methodology; both GENIAC and the Japan AI Safety Institute operate under the mandate the Plan sets. Third, economic security integration: breaking from previous plans, the 7th Plan explicitly aligns science and technology strategy with economic security objectives, identifying strategically sensitive technology domains, introducing research security and integrity requirements for universities, and adopting a selective rather than uniformly open approach to international collaboration. Attracting global talent and positioning Japan as an international innovation hub are also explicit goals.

items.title: Open Innovation Promotion Tax System
items.original_name: オープンイノベーション促進税制
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.document_name: オープンイノベーション促進税制
items.body:
A Japanese income-deduction / deductible-expense incentive that supports corporate–startup open innovation by allowing eligible corporations to deduct up to 25% of the acquisition cost of qualifying startup shares, subject to conditions and limits.

Introduced as part of the FY2020 Tax Reform (effective 1 April 2020) and administered by METI and the National Tax Agency, the Open Innovation Promotion Tax System allows eligible blue-return corporations to deduct 25% of the acquisition cost of qualifying startup shares from taxable income in the year of acquisition, subject to statutory conditions. The deducted amount is booked to a special account and reversed into taxable income if defined trigger events occur (such as disposal of shares). Investment thresholds: a minimum of ¥100M for acquisitions in domestic Japanese startups; ¥500M for foreign-based startups; ¥10M for SMEs investing in domestic startups. The target startup must be unlisted, incorporated, and have commenced operations within the past 10 years. An M&A-type variant was added for transactions from 1 April 2023, covering majority voting-right control acquisitions. Under the FY2026 Tax Reform Outline (agreed 19 December 2025, enacted March 2026), the application period was extended by a further two years, moving the end date from 31 March 2026 to 31 March 2028.

items.title: IPA MITOU Program
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
A national Japanese talent development programme run by IPA/METI since FY2000, discovering and developing young IT and AI innovators through intensive mentorship, project-based funding, and a Super Creator recognition system.

The MITOU Program (Exploratory IT Human Resources Project; officially 未踏IT人材発掘・育成事業) was launched by METI in FY2000 and is operated by the Information-technology Promotion Agency (IPA). The programme's mission is to discover and develop exceptional young IT creators capable of driving innovation in AI, robotics, big data, and other frontier digital technologies. As of April 2025, the programme has developed over 2,300 'Creators'. The MITOU Programme has three tracks: MITOU IT Program — for IT talents under age 25 (approx. 9 months); focuses on big data, AI, robotics, and novel digital products; MITOU Advanced Program — for aspiring IT entrepreneurs of all ages (approx. 8 months); adds business advisors alongside technical project managers; targets commercialisation and startup creation; MITOU Target Program — for specialists of all ages (up to 18 months); targets specific frontier technology areas designated annually (past themes include quantum computing, AI, reservoir computing). All tracks share a core model: 'Project Managers' — prominent Japanese IT innovators from academia and industry — select promising individuals from applicants, mentor them intensively through weekly one-to-one sessions, and guide project development. Creators retain IP rights from their projects. Outstanding performers are designated 'Super Creators' by METI. Graduates have founded over 250 businesses and commercialised numerous AI products. The MITOU Foundation (established 2014 by alumni) extends the programme's community and runs MITOU Junior for innovators aged 17 and under. Annual programme budget is not publicly itemised but sits within IPA's total budget (JPY 146.4B as of April 2025 across all programmes).

items.title: DX Investment Promotion Tax Incentive
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
A Japanese corporate tax credit providing up to 5% of eligible cloud/AI investment costs (with a ceiling of 20% of annual corporate tax liability) for companies with government-approved digital transformation plans under the Industrial Competitiveness Enhancement Act.

The DX Investment Promotion Tax System (DX投資促進税制) was introduced in the FY2022 tax reform, effective from 2 August 2021, and has subsequently been revised and extended. It applies to companies that have obtained 'DX Certification' from METI and have a business plan certified under the Industrial Competitiveness Enhancement Act (ICEA) that sets out investments in cloud services, AI systems, and digital infrastructure to achieve digital transformation across the enterprise. Eligible companies may choose between: a 5% tax credit on qualifying investment costs; or a 30% special depreciation allowance on qualifying assets. The tax credit is subject to a ceiling of 20% of annual corporate tax liability (bundled with the Carbon Neutrality investment credit). Eligible investments include: cloud computing migrations; enterprise AI system deployments; DX-related software and data infrastructure; and digital platform integration. The 2025 Tax Reform Act extended the regime by three years, to fiscal years beginning on or before 1 April 2028, while increasing the minimum qualifying investment size from JPY 20M to JPY 100M, and reducing the special depreciation rate for machinery and equipment from 40% to 35%. The programme is designed to incentivise large-scale, cross-departmental digital transformation rather than point-solution technology adoption.

items.title: AI and Semiconductor Industry Strengthening Framework
items.original_name: AI and Semiconductor Industry Strengthening Framework AI・半導体産業強化フレームワーク
items.category: Regulations, guidelines and standards
items.document_name: AI and Semiconductor Industry Strengthening Framework AI・半導体産業強化フレームワーク
items.body:
A Cabinet-approved comprehensive Japanese policy framework committing over JPY 10 trillion in public support for AI and semiconductor sectors by FY2030, targeting JPY 50 trillion+ in combined public-private investment over the next decade.

Approved by the Japanese Cabinet as part of the 'Comprehensive Economic Measures for Ensuring National Security and Sustainable Growth' on 22 November 2024, the AI and Semiconductor Industry Strengthening Framework is Japan's overarching policy commitment to reassert global leadership in AI and semiconductor technologies. The framework covers the seven-year period to FY2030. Core elements include: (1) Over JPY 10 trillion in cumulative public support for AI and semiconductor R&D, infrastructure, and production, delivered through subsidies administered by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI), NEDO programmes, and direct investment vehicles; (2) A target of inducing more than JPY 50 trillion in combined public-private investment over the next decade; (3) From FY2026, METI nearly quadrupled its annual AI and semiconductor budget to approximately JPY 1.23 trillion, up from approximately JPY 330B in FY2025; (4) Key beneficiaries include Rapidus (JPY 920B+ for 2nm chip production at Hokkaido), TSMC Japan (Kumamoto fabs), and five companies receiving JPY 72.5B in AI supercomputer development grants (Sakura Internet, KDDI, and others); (5) A new JPY 1T annual investment from the regular budget (from FY2026), signalling long-term commitment rather than one-off supplementary spending; (6) Specific FY2025 components include JPY 40B for innovative AI semiconductor fundamental research, JPY 1.05T for next-generation chip and quantum computing, and JPY 471.4B for domestic chip production support. The framework is implemented through METI, NEDO, and the New Form of Capitalism Realisation Council, with Japan's Growth Strategy Headquarters — chaired by the Prime Minister — serving as oversight body.

items.title: AI Strategic Headquarters
items.category: National – AI governance bodies or mechanisms
items.body:
Central government body responsible for coordinating Japan’s national AI strategy.

The AI Strategic Headquarters oversees the implementation of Japan’s national AI strategy and coordinates policy across ministries, agencies, and research institutions. The body is responsible for setting strategic priorities, promoting AI research and innovation, and ensuring that government initiatives align with national technological goals. Its responsibilities include developing national AI roadmaps, promoting collaboration between academia and industry, and supporting the development of ethical AI governance frameworks. The headquarters also plays a role in coordinating international AI cooperation and guiding investment in research infrastructure and innovation programmes.

items.title: Law No. 5321/2026 – Measures for the Implementation of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 (Artificial Intelligence Act), Amendment of Law 4961/2022, and Other Provisions
items.original_name: Μέτρα εφαρμογής του Κανονισμού (ΕΕ) 2024/1689 του Ευρωπαϊκού Κοινοβουλίου και του Συμβουλίου της 13ης Ιουνίου 2024 (Κανονισμός για την Τεχνητή Νοημοσύνη) - Τροποποίηση του ν. 4961/2022 και άλλες διατάξεις
items.category: Regulations, guidelines and standards
items.document_name: Μέτρα εφαρμογής του Κανονισμού (ΕΕ) 2024/1689 του Ευρωπαϊκού Κοινοβουλίου και του Συμβουλίου της 13ης Ιουνίου 2024 (Κανονισμός για την Τεχνητή Νοημοσύνη) - Τροποποίηση του ν. 4961/2022 και άλλες διατάξεις
items.body: Law No. 5321/2026 establishes the national framework for the implementation of the EU ΑΙ Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) in Greece. It designates competent authorities, provides for market surveillance and enforcement, establishes an AI regulatory sandbox, a AI Systems Registry for the public sector and an AI Observatory, and promotes the trustworthy and innovative use of AI. The law further replaces the AI governance provisions previously contained in Law 4961/2022.

items.title: Justice Practical Guide
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
The Justice Practical Guide is a digital tool that helps citizens and businesses quickly find clear and simple information about justice‑related services in everyday language. It was created to make access to justice faster and more understandable, reducing the need to visit onsite services and helping navigate common legal situations. It uses AI to provide quick, natural‑language answers, ensuring that anyone - regardless of legal knowledge - can understand the options available to them.

The Justice Practical Guide (Guia Prático da Justiça – GPJ) was created to address a persistent challenge in the justice system: citizens often struggle to understand legal information and the steps required to solve common justice-related issues. By simplifying and centralising information about procedures – such as contracts, family matters, consumer rights, mediation, and peace-court processes – the GPJ helps reduce informational barriers and prevents unnecessary travel to justice services. It builds on the principle that access to justice begins with clear, accessible information that helps people make informed decisions about their rights. 
The initiative’s main objective is to offer a single, intuitive digital channel where citizens and businesses can quickly obtain answers written in clear, everyday language. To achieve this, in a few months, the GPJ will aggregate content from approximately 190 services available on the Digital Portal of Justice (Plataforma Digital da Justiça) and transform complex legal concepts into simple explanations. It’s an AI‑based engine – built, until now, on GPT‑4 models and reinforced with a curated legal knowledge base – providing natural‑language responses validated by justice experts to ensure accuracy and reliability. This combination of structured content and expert‑supervised AI aims to reduce information asymmetry and make justice services more understandable for all. 
Over time, the GPJ has evolved from a static guidance tool into an intelligent conversational assistant (“Bot”), capable of helping users identify the correct service or procedure for their situation. The new version also incorporates mechanisms for user feedback, enabling continuous improvement and reinforcing human oversight in the decision‑making loop. By integrating with systems such as google maps and SIGA (platform for shedulling onsite appointments), the GPJ strengthens interoperability across justice services and enhances the user experience across web and mobile channels. 
Looking ahead, the initiative is designed to scale. Future development includes expanding coverage to all 190 justice services, improving content governance processes, and ensuring regular updates as legislation and procedures evolve. Internally, the project is becoming institutionalised through structured governance models, dedicated teams, and alignment with wider digital-transformation programmes within the Ministry of Justice. As the platform matures, it is expected to extend it’s reach, support multilingual interaction, and serve as a model for replicating AI-enhanced public-service guidance across other sectors of government.

items.title: Frontier AI Initiative
items.category: AI Policy Frameworks and Initiatives (intergovernmental or supranational)
items.body:
An EU initiative to coordinate research, infrastructure and governance efforts around frontier artificial intelligence systems and strengthen Europe’s ability to develop and deploy highly capable AI models.

The Frontier AI Initiative was introduced by the European Commission as part of the EU’s broader “Apply AI Strategy” and AI Continent policy framework. Its objective is to strengthen Europe’s capabilities in developing and governing frontier-level AI systems. Activities include convening expert forums, coordinating research investments, aligning safety and evaluation approaches, and linking existing European high-performance computing facilities with emerging AI development ecosystems. The initiative also aims to reduce Europe’s reliance on foreign frontier models by supporting domestic research capacity and enabling collaboration between public laboratories, startups and established technology companies. In addition, the programme promotes responsible development by embedding safety testing, benchmarking and governance mechanisms into the development pipeline for advanced models. The Frontier AI Initiative therefore acts as both a coordination mechanism and an enabling platform for European investment in advanced AI capabilities.

items.title: EU Scaleup Europe Fund
items.category: AI Policy Frameworks and Initiatives (intergovernmental or supranational)
items.body:
The Scaleup Europe Fund is a multi-billion-euro, privately managed and publicly anchored growth capital fund announced by the European Commission in October 2025, aimed at investing in the most promising European companies in strategic deep tech areas, including artificial intelligence, quantum technologies, semiconductors, robotics, energy, space, and biotechnologies.

The Scaleup Europe Fund responds to Europe's well-documented late-stage funding gap, in which promising companies have struggled to access the growth capital needed to compete with US and Asian peers. The fund operates as a market-based, privately managed and privately co-financed growth vehicle, focusing on late-stage and growth capital investments in major European-led investment rounds across strategic deep tech sectors. The Commission is a founding investor alongside a group of leading European institutional investors announced on 28 October 2025, including Novo Holdings, EIFO (Denmark), CriteriaCaixa, Santander/Mouro Capital, Fondazione Compagnia San Paolo/Intesa Sanpaolo/Fondazione Cariplo, APG Asset Management (on behalf of Dutch pension fund ABP), Wallenberg Investments, and BGK (Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego). An independent fund manager is being selected through a public call for expressions of interest (closed February 2026); appointment is expected in April 2026. A second fundraising round will follow to diversify the investor base.

items.title: EU General-Purpose AI (GPAI) Code of Practice
items.category: AI Policy Frameworks and Initiatives (intergovernmental or supranational)
items.body:
A co-regulatory instrument under Article 56 of the EU AI Act, developed through a multi-stakeholder process led by the EU AI Office, which translates the AI Act's obligations for General Purpose AI (GPAI) model providers into specific, operationalisable compliance measures covering transparency, copyright, systemic risk assessment, safety testing, incident reporting and governance.

The GPAI Code of Practice is one of the most consequential instruments under the EU AI Act for frontier AI model developers, as it directly operationalises the obligations in Chapter V of the Act for providers of general-purpose AI models. The Code was developed through an unprecedented multi-stakeholder drafting process coordinated by the EU AI Office, running from November 2024. It involved over 1,000 stakeholders including AI developers (OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Meta, Anthropic, Mistral, Aleph Alpha and others), academic researchers, civil society organisations, standards bodies, and national competent authorities. Draft versions were published iteratively with a final adopted version targeted for May 2025. The Code is structured across four substantive chapters: transparency and copyright obligations (requiring model documentation, training data disclosure, compliance with EU copyright law, and reservation of rights mechanisms); safety and security for non-systemic-risk models; additional systemic risk obligations (covering adversarial testing, red-teaming, cybersecurity measures, serious incident reporting, and model evaluations against safety benchmarks); and governance and accountability. The Code includes specific "measures" and "key performance indicators" for each obligation, enabling both self-assessment by providers and external verification by the AI Office. Compliance with the Code creates a presumption of conformity under the AI Act, substantially reducing legal uncertainty for GPAI providers. Non-compliance with GPAI obligations under the AI Act (where the Code applies) can result in fines of up to EUR 15 million or 3% of global annual turnover.

items.title: EU AI Office
items.category: AI Governance Bodies and Mechanisms (intergovernmental or supranational)
items.body:
The European Commission body responsible for overseeing the implementation and enforcement of the EU AI Act at the EU level, with specific responsibility for supervising General Purpose AI (GPAI) models and systemic risk assessment.

The EU AI Office was established by European Commission Decision on 24 January 2024, ahead of the formal entry into force of the EU AI Act (August 2024), in recognition of the need for a dedicated EU-level body to coordinate AI Act implementation and provide specialised technical and governance expertise. Its mandate is broader than enforcement alone: the AI Office serves as the EU's primary institutional voice on AI policy, representing the Commission in international AI forums including the OECD, G7, G20, the Council of Europe, ISO/IEC, and the International Network of AI Safety Institutes. The AI Office has four main functions. First, AI Act implementation and enforcement: it is the sole competent authority for supervising GPAI model providers across the EU, including conducting conformity assessments, requesting model evaluations, issuing warnings and, where necessary, imposing fines (up to EUR 15 million or 3% of global annual turnover for GPAI violations). Second, standards and guidance: it coordinates with European standards bodies (CEN/CENELEC, ETSI) on harmonised standards for AI Act compliance and publishes guidelines, codes of practice and technical documentation requirements. Third, the Office leads the multi-stakeholder drafting process for the GPAI Code of Practice, a key implementation instrument for GPAI model providers under Article 56 of the AI Act. Fourth, AI research and safety: the Office conducts and commissions research on AI safety risks, including systemic risks from GPAI models, and maintains the EU's scientific capacity for AI evaluation. It also manages the Apply AI Alliance under the Apply AI Strategy and coordinates AI Factories network development under InvestAI.

items.title: EU AI Continent Action Plan
items.category: AI Policy Frameworks and Initiatives (intergovernmental or supranational)
items.body:
The European Commission's AI strategy adopted in 2025, setting out a multi-pillar framework to make Europe "an AI Continent". The Plan encompasses 5 strategic pillars: computing infrastructure and data, AI research and innovation talent, the regulatory environment, AI adoption across sectors, and European AI sovereignty and global outreach. It serves as the parent strategic framework for InvestAI, the Apply AI Strategy, the AI Factories network, and the EU AI Office's coordination mandate.

The AI Continent Action Plan was announced by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on 11 February 2025 at the Paris AI Action Summit alongside the InvestAI initiative. It operates around five pillars. Pillar one (computing and data): mobilise EUR 200 billion in AI investment through InvestAI, build five AI gigafactories, expand the 19 AI Factories network through EuroHPC, and develop the European common data spaces. Pillar two (talent and skills): retain AI researchers and engineers in Europe, attract global talent, and build a pipeline of AI-skilled workers at all levels through actions under the Pact for Skills and the Digital Education Action Plan. Pillar three (regulatory environment): ensure the AI Act is implemented in a way that is clear, predictable and minimises unnecessary compliance burdens for innovators, including SMEs; streamline Member State transposition; and develop harmonised standards rapidly. Pillar four (AI adoption): operationalise the Apply AI Strategy across 11 priority sectors; deploy the European Digital Innovation Hubs network for SME support; and establish the Apply AI Alliance to coordinate public-private uptake. Pillar five (sovereignty and outreach): build European leadership in trustworthy AI; strengthen bilateral AI partnerships with the US, UK, Japan, Canada and others; and promote the EU's regulatory model in multilateral forums.

items.title: Voucher Cloud & Cybersecurity
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
A ministerial voucher programme to subsidise the purchase/subscription of cloud and cybersecurity services by SMEs and self-employed persons (eligible products explicitly include cloud SaaS with integrated AI features such as productivity/ERP/CRM tools). The measure reduces infrastructure and security barriers for SMEs adopting AI-enabled software.

The Voucher Cloud & Cybersecurity programme is a demand-side subsidy instrument operated by the Ministero delle Imprese e del Made in Italy (MIMIT). It provides vouchers to eligible SMEs and self-employed persons (lavoratori autonomi) to offset the cost of purchasing or subscribing to cloud computing and cybersecurity services from a register of prequalified suppliers. Eligible products explicitly include cloud SaaS solutions with integrated AI features meaning the programme directly lowers the financial barrier to SME adoption of AI-enabled software without requiring beneficiaries to procure AI separately. Supplier preregistration opened on 27 February 2026, establishing the pool of eligible vendors from which SMEs may choose; the SME application window ran from March to April 2026. The programme complements Italy's broader SME digitalisation strategy, including the national Competence Centers network and the Transition 5.0 incentive scheme.

items.title: Virtual assistant in mObywatel
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
The virtual assistant in mObywatel is an AI chatbot, powered by a Polish LLM (PLLuM), available through a national digital citizen app. It was created in order to make information about public services more available to citizens. It is meant to combat digital exclusion and provide a safe and verified alternative to general purpose chatbots in the official context.

The Virtual Assistant is an attempt to help the citizen navigate the multitude of available public services ranging from reporting an environmental violations, to registering the birth of a child. Every year many services are introduced, changed, or retired, making it difficult for the citizen to keep track of them. The ability to ask questions in natural language makes the services more approachable, and by extension helps every citizen access everything the modern state has to offer. As a secondary objective, the initiative strives to build trusted public AI – both in the terms of the information provided by the Virtual Assistant, and by legally and technically enshrining the safety of the citizen data. 

The virtual assistant differs from the commercial offerings by the strict validation and verification of the knowledge sources and close integration with government databases. The answers it provides are limited to the official documentation – it is also designed not to give opinions or judgement-based advice. This ensures the assistant can be trusted to help citizens, while at the same time saving the budgetary cost of citizens asking general-knowledge questions. Furthermore, the assistant is embedded in mObywatel - the official Polish state application that lets people keep digital versions of important documents and use many public services safely on their mobiles. Therefore, if the user asks about a service or a document available in the app, the assistant can link directly to that service, ensuring seamless user experience. 

Finally, the Virtual Assistant is designed from the ground up to be privacy-preserving. It does not link the conversations to a user preventing any profiling. Every message goes through a multi-step process designed to purge any personally identifiable information. The LLM infrastructure is fully self-managed, to prevent external API providers from accessing the conversation data. 

The Virtual Assistant has been used 600 000 times in the two months from its introduction. The performance of the assistant is measured in real time, based on the user feedback (surveys after a conversation and the ability to up and downvote specific answers). Specific answers receive 62% positive votes and 38% negative, while the whole conversations have an equal split of 44% good or very good and 44% of bad or very bad. The specific rated conversations and messages are then assessed both manually and automatically by analytical and data science teams to guide the development of the system. Moreover, the project is assessed using social science frameworks, i.e: moderated workshops and unmoderated online forms.

items.title: The Interministerial AI Assistant
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
The AI Assistant is a secure chat tool for public servants, designed to help them write, summarize and find information faster. It was developed to give government teams an easy and trusted way to use generative AI in their daily work. The goal is to improve efficiency while reducing duplicated efforts across ministries.

The AI Assistant is a secure, government-wide chat tool designed for public servants. It helps users draft and improve text, summarize long documents, and answer day-to-day questions more quickly, while keeping a clear focus on safe and responsible use in a public administration context. The initiative was developed to address a growing need across ministries: many teams were exploring generative AI, but often with separate tools and duplicated technical efforts. By providing a shared assistant, the government aims to make AI easier to access for public servants, reduce fragmentation, and support productivity gains in routine tasks.

In 2025, the AI Assistant was piloted across 8 ministries with up to 10,000 volunteer users. It helped public servants draft, summarize and search information faster, supporting everyday work and reducing the need for separate ministry-by-ministry tools. Impact has been tracked through user adoption (registrations and active use), usage statistics (queries, features used), and qualitative feedback from pilot administrations. Future results are expected to include wider adoption, more time saved on routine tasks, and improved consistency and security in how generative AI is used across government.

Key challenges included ensuring strong security and compliance for government use, scaling computing capacity cost-effectively, and building trust among users. Another risk was fragmentation, with ministries developing separate assistants and duplicating effort. These challenges were addressed by hosting the service on secure infrastructure, monitoring usage to manage costs, and designing the Assistant as a shared tool that can evolve with ministry needs. Lessons learned include the importance of starting with clear, high-value everyday tasks (writing, summarising), providing user guidance and support, and collecting feedback early to improve the service. Success depends on reliable performance, strong governance, and gradual scaling based on real adoption.

Over time, the AI Assistant is expected to expand its user base and offer more advanced features, including stronger connections to trusted public information sources and the ability to work with internal document collections. It is designed to scale progressively, in line with security requirements and real usage needs, while remaining interoperable with other government digital tools.

items.title: Tampere Pulse – AI-Driven Visitor Flow Forecasting for Smarter Urban Decision-Making (Subnational: City of Tampere)
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
Tampere Pulse is an AI-powered predictive analytics service developed by the City of Tampere, Finland, to forecast visitor flows in the urban centre. By leveraging anonymised IoT and machine vision data, it predicts foot traffic up to one month in advance, enabling authorities and businesses to enact smarter decision-making, operational planning, resource allocation, and public services through human-centric, trustworthy AI.

Tampere Pulse is an AI-enabled urban analytics initiative developed by the City of Tampere to improve evidence-based decision-making related to visitor flows in the city centre. The initiative addresses a common challenge faced by cities: limited real-time and forward-looking insight into how people move through urban environments, particularly during events, seasonal changes, or extreme weather conditions. By transforming anonymised sensor data into predictive insights, Tampere Pulse enables public authorities and local stakeholders to better anticipate demand, manage public spaces, and optimise services while respecting privacy and ethical standards. 

The primary objective of the initiative is to support smarter, more responsive urban governance through reliable short- and medium-term forecasts of pedestrian volumes. The system combines AI-based predictive models with multiple data sources, including anonymised camera-based counts, weather data, temporal patterns, and event information. The resulting forecasts help city departments, local businesses, and other stakeholders to plan resources, staffing, maintenance, safety measures, and mobility services more effectively. A key objective is to strengthen human-AI collaboration by presenting predictions through an intuitive, map-based interface that supports interpretation and informed decision-making rather than automated action.  

The key stakeholders include companies, which act as both customers and co-creators of the service; city residents and visitors, who can use the service to plan routes during peak hours and identify quieter or livelier areas of the city; maintenance teams, for whom the service supports more efficient scheduling and allocation of work; and security teams, which can use the insights to prepare for high-traffic periods and ensure appropriate staffing and readiness. Importantly, the solution is designed in line with principles of trustworthy and human-centric AI: data is anonymised at source, model limitations are communicated transparently, and the system is used as a decision-support tool rather than a substitute for human judgement. Additionally, the AI-forecast data can be leveraged for security and risk-preparedness purposes, with scalable potential to create a safer city ecosystem.

items.title: Sectoral Workforce Solutions Program (AI-focused projects)
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
A dedicated CAD 50M federal contribution programme funding sectoral organisations to develop and deliver skills training for workers in industries potentially disrupted by AI, helping them reskill and adapt to an AI-transformed labour market.

The AI stream of the Sectoral Workforce Solutions Program (SWSP) was announced in Canada's Budget 2024, allocating CAD 50M over four years (2025–26 to 2028–29) to support workers who may be impacted by AI through new skills training in potentially disrupted sectors and communities. The SWSP itself was originally established in Budget 2021 with CAD 960M over three years and has since invested over CAD 560M across 55 projects, supporting training for over 115,000 participants. The programme is administered by Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) and funds not-for-profit organisations, for-profit organisations, municipal governments, Indigenous organisations, and provincial/territorial bodies that have demonstrated knowledge of sectoral skills issues and established partnerships with national, regional, or local sectoral stakeholders. Projects must address workforce development needs in key sectors (agriculture/agri-food, construction, health, ICT, manufacturing, natural resources and environment, tourism, and transportation) and at minimum 10% co-funding from non-ESDC sources is required. The AI stream specifically targets workers facing job displacement or skills gaps due to AI adoption. Eligible activities include training and reskilling, attracting and retaining workforce, developing sector-wide standards and tools, and implementing creative workforce solutions. Funding per project ranges from CAD 5M to CAD 50M. Projects are national (spanning three+ provinces) or regional in scope.

items.title: R&D & Innovation Tax Credit 4.0
items.original_name: Credito d'Imposta in Ricerca, Sviluppo, Innovazione e Design 4.0
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.document_name: Credito d'Imposta in Ricerca, Sviluppo, Innovazione e Design 4.0
items.body:
A national Italian tax credit scheme established under Law 160/2019 to support business investments in research and development (R&D), technological innovation, design, and digital transformation as part of the Transition Plan 4.0. The scheme provides a 10% tax credit for R&D activities and a 5% tax credit for innovation and design activities, applicable to companies of all sizes operating in Italy.

Italy’s R&D and Innovation Tax Credit—established under Transition Plan 4.0 through Budget Law 2020 (Law 160/2019)—provides targeted tax incentives supporting business investments in research, technological development, design, and digital transformation. The scheme grants a 10% volume‑based tax credit for eligible R&D activities, as confirmed by the OECD INNOTAX Portal, which recognises this rate as part of Italy’s current national R&D incentive framework. Alongside R&D support, Italy also offers a 5% tax credit for technological innovation, design, and creative activities for fiscal years 2024–2025, as documented by professional tax analysts examining the 2025 incentive measures. These credits apply broadly to all companies operating in Italy, including permanent establishments of non‑resident entities, without restrictions related to company size, sector, or legal form. Together, these incentives form a core component of Italy’s industrial modernization agenda, encouraging companies to integrate advanced digital technologies—such as artificial intelligence, automation, and cloud computing—into their production and innovation processes as part of their transition to Industry 4.0 and beyond.

items.title: Public Sector AI Community of Practice
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
New Zealand’s Public Sector AI Community of Practice is an active professional network of digital government practitioners meeting monthly online for wide knowledge sharing, learning and connection. Online meetings regularly bring together up to 200 practitioners from a wide range of government organisations to share knowledge on a range of AI-related topics and relevant information.

The Public Sector AI Community of Practice is a centrally led professional network that connects digital practitioners across New Zealand’s wider public sector. In its first full year, membership expanded from 60 to 95 agencies nationwide, with more than 600 practitioners engaged overall. Around 200 practitioners typically join each monthly online session, and the community delivered more than a dozen sessions over the year. Its purpose is to provide a shared space where agencies can learn from one another, explore emerging technologies and strengthen capability across government.
As part of the Government Chief Digital Officer’s AI Work Programme, the community’s agenda is shaped by members’ interests and feedback, ensuring sessions remain timely and relevant. Each monthly gathering is built around the themes of share, learn and connect, combining formal presentations, knowledge‑sharing updates and structured discussions. Agencies routinely present updates on their AI programmes and initiatives, offering insights into practical implementation, lessons learned and developing responsible AI practices. Deep‑dive sessions explore technical topics or emerging developments, often led by subject‑matter experts such as data platform managers and scientists who share specialist knowledge or support training.
Sessions examine active AI use cases and pilots, provide visibility into early exploratory projects and highlight shifts in technology or the operating environment that affect government AI adoption. Sub‑communities have begun to form around shared areas of practice, including a growing Policy Professionals group led by practitioners in the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet.

items.title: Piano Transizione 4.0 – Tax Credit
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
An Italian tax credit scheme for investments in Industry 4.0 tangible capital goods (including AI-integrated machinery) of up to 20% of eligible costs, with a national spending cap of EUR 2.2B for 2025.

Rooted in the original Industria 4.0 plan (Law 232/2016), the Transizione 4.0 tax credit has been the primary Italian fiscal incentive for industrial digital transformation. For investments in new tangible 4.0 capital goods (Annex A of Law 232/2016 — interconnected machinery, computer-controlled systems, IoT devices, AI and robotics equipment) made between 1 January 2025 and 31 December 2025 (or booked by 31 December 2025 with at least 20% down payment and completed by 30 June 2026), the 2025 Budget Law introduced: a 20% credit on investment portions up to EUR 2.5M; 10% on portions from EUR 2.5M to EUR 10M; 5% on portions from EUR 10M to EUR 20M. A national aggregate spending cap of EUR 2.2B for 2025 was introduced; companies submit communications to MIMIT via the GSE portal on a first-come-first-served basis and credits are suspended once the cap is reached (this occurred in November 2025). The 2025 Budget Law largely terminated the credit for new intangible investments in 2025, retaining eligibility only for assets connected to qualifying tangible investments already booked by 31 December 2024. The incompatibility with the Transizione 5.0 credit is confirmed. From 2026, the regime transitions to an enhanced depreciation (hyper-depreciation) system under Budget Law 2026. Target audience: Italian companies across all productive sectors investing in digital 4.0 production assets.

items.title: OTT2 : Dynamic Data-Driven Personalisation of Employment Services and Counsellor Decision Support
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
OTT2 is an AI-powered decision support system that helps Estonia’s Unemployment Insurance Fund prevent long-term unemployment. It combines data from public registries to assess each jobseeker’s employment prospects in real time, enabling counsellors to identify those at highest risk and focus support where it is most needed. With above 98% forecast accuracy, it eliminates laborious and error-prone manual work and it enables a policy pilot to dedicate counselling resource to high-risk customers.

Estonia’s public employment service faces the same challenge seen worldwide: allocating limited support to jobseekers with very different needs. Before 2020, counsellors relied on rules of thumb, personal experience and the manual profiling of roughly 45 indicators ranging from demographic characteristics and work history to health status and local labour‑market conditions. In practice, this volume of information was difficult to process consistently, making it hard to reliably identify people at risk of long‑term unemployment and in need of more intensive support.

This changed with the introduction of OTT1 in 2020, Estonia’s first data‑driven decision‑support tool for counsellors. Using a machine‑learning model, it assessed each jobseeker’s employment prospects at the point of registration. Over several years of operational use, the Estonian Unemployment Insurance Fund (EUIF) strengthened the model, built organisational confidence and gathered the evidence needed to expand its approach. OTT2 represents this next step. Whereas OTT1 produced a single assessment at registration, OTT2 generates dynamic, regularly updated assessments that reflect changes in a jobseeker’s situation—such as completing training or missing an assigned activity—so counsellors can make decisions using the most current information. The model is retrained periodically on new data but does not change autonomously, ensuring stability, transparency and auditability in a high‑stakes service. OTT2 also explains the main factors shaping each prediction and how these evolve over time, helping counsellors interpret results and offer more personalised support.

OTT2 builds on the strong performance of its predecessor, which achieved over 95% prediction accuracy. By updating assessments as circumstances change, accuracy is expected to rise above 98%; this is being tested in a 2026 pilot. The pilot also introduces a targeted service change: the approximately 20% of newly registered jobseekers identified as lowest‑risk will no longer receive mandatory counselling, allowing counsellors to focus more time on individuals at higher risk of long‑term unemployment. Even small reductions in unemployment duration have significant fiscal impact—one day less is estimated to save around 3.8% of annual expenditure.

items.title: Nuova Sabatini Digital
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
An Italian government programme subsidising the interest costs on bank or leasing loans taken by SMEs to purchase new capital goods including AI-integrated machinery, hardware, software, and digital 4.0 technologies.

The 'Nuova Sabatini' (officially: Beni Strumentali – Nuova Sabatini) is administered by MIMIT and is Italy's principal instrument for facilitating SME access to credit for productive investments. The mechanism: an SME applies for a bank loan or financial leasing for eligible assets (new factory machinery, equipment, plants, hardware, software, digital technologies); MIMIT then provides a capital grant (contributo in conto impianti) equivalent to a 2.75% interest subsidy on a conventional five-year loan of equal amount. For investments in Industry 4.0 technologies (including AI, IoT, robotics, augmented reality, big data, cloud computing — defined by Annex A/B criteria), the subsidy is enhanced to 3.575% per year (the 'Sabatini Digital' or '4.0' track). For green investments, the same enhanced 3.575% rate applies. The minimum loan is EUR 20,000; the maximum is EUR 4M per VAT number. Applications are submitted digitally via MIMIT's platform; the bank/intermediary assesses creditworthiness and forwards to MIMIT. The Budget Law 2025 refinanced Nuova Sabatini with EUR 1.7B for 2025–2029; the Budget Law 2026 separately allocated EUR 650M for 2026–2027. Can be combined with the Fondo di Garanzia PMI. Target audience: micro, small, and medium-sized Italian enterprises across all productive sectors (excluding financial and insurance activities).

items.title: National Data Infrastructure (NDI)
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
The National Data Infrastructure (NDI) constitutes a set of norms, policies, architectures, standards, technological tools, and information assets, aimed at promoting the strategic use of data held by the bodies and entities of the Brazilian Federal Executive Branch. The IND enables data discovery, interoperability, access, strategic use, privacy, security, and protection. The objective is to improve public service, empower citizens, and promote economic and social development.

The National Data Infrastructure (NDI) was created to address a long‑standing challenge in Brazil’s Federal Public Administration: public data is often dispersed across different systems, formats, and technological standards, limiting its usefulness for evidence‑based policymaking, efficient service delivery, and transparent information sharing. Fragmentation and limited interoperability have historically prevented government bodies from fully realizing the value of the information they collect and maintain.
The NDI aims to transform this landscape by promoting the strategic use of data across the federal government. Its purpose is to ensure that public bodies can discover, access, and integrate data securely and responsibly, turning information into actionable insights for policy development. The initiative supports the interoperability, privacy, security, and protection of public data, helping institutions improve services, empower citizens, and foster economic and social development. It also contributes to national sovereignty and federative integration by establishing a trusted environment for data use while rationalizing public-sector costs. In aligning itself with international best practices, the NDI strengthens Brazil’s capacity for data-driven decision-making and technological innovation.
Formally instituted by Decree No. 12,198 on September 24, 2024, the NDI represents an evolution of the National Open Data Infrastructure established in 2016. While the earlier initiative focused primarily on open data, the NDI expands the scope to include interoperability, governance, security, privacy, and digital public goods, reflecting a more comprehensive approach to public-sector data management.
NDI initiatives are integrated into the Federal Digital Government Strategy, which is updated annually. Its ongoing implementation is supported by several mechanisms. These include the development of data‑governance and sharing policies, which undergo public consultation; the adoption of common technological models such as the Government Cloud, which standardizes infrastructure and data integration practices; the expansion of interoperable national data catalogs to organize and make thousands of datasets reusable; and the consolidation of specialized roles, such as data executives, within government structures. Together, these measures support a gradual, scalable rollout that can expand to additional levels of government and new data partners.

items.title: MEB Smart Legislation Assistant  (AI-powered Legal Assistant)
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
The MEB Smart Legislation Assistant is an AI-powered tool that helps Ministry staff quickly access and understand official legislation. It allows users to ask questions in plain language and receive structured answers supported by official legal sources. The system reduces time spent searching complex legal texts and improves accuracy in administrative decision-making.

The MEB Smart Legislation Assistant is an artificial intelligence–based decision support system developed by the Directorate General for Innovation and Educational Technologies to improve access to legislation within the Ministry of National Education. Ministry staff are required to consult thousands of pages of laws, regulations, circulars and guidelines in their daily work, which is time-consuming and prone to error. The initiative addresses this challenge by providing fast, reliable and transparent access to up-to-date legal information.

The system allows authorised users to ask legal questions in natural language without requiring technical or legal expertise. Using advanced language models, the assistant searches official legislation sources and presents answers in a structured and understandable format. Each response is supported by direct references to the relevant legal provisions, enabling users to verify information through official sources such as mevzuat.gov.tr.

Security and trust are central to the initiative. Access is restricted to authorised Ministry personnel and integrated with existing authentication infrastructure. The system operates only on verified and official legal texts and provides transparency by showing how answers are generated, including which legal documents and articles were used.

The initiative is designed as a continuously evolving system. Through user feedback and performance analytics, the assistant is regularly improved to enhance accuracy, coverage and usability. In the future, the system is expected to expand its scope to include additional legal documents, institutional guidelines and internal regulatory content, contributing to a broader AI ecosystem within the Ministry.

items.title: KB Lab
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
KB-labb (The KBLab) at the National Library of Sweden is a data-driven infrastructure for research. It provides access to the library’s massive digital collections—including newspapers, books, and radio/TV—for large-scale analysis.

KBLab is a national infrastructure for data-driven research, established by the Royal Library (KB). The initiative aims to bridge the gap between large-scale digitized cultural heritage and traditional humanities methods. As collections reach petabyte levels – encompassing everything from historical newspapers to social media and audiovisual broadcasts – manual analysis becomes impossible. KBLab makes this "big data" accessible through computational tools and high-performance environments, transforming the library from a place for reading to an arena for active computing.

The main goal is to lower the thresholds for KB's digital vault. Through a "co-design" environment, the lab facilitates the development of large-scale AI models, especially language (LLM) and vision models trained on Swedish material. These models function as a "digital public good" that enables complex analyses, such as entity recognition and structural mapping in millions of documents. The aim is to create an ecosystem where computer science and humanities meet to generate new knowledge from cultural heritage. From being a pilot project, KBLab has become a central pillar of KB's digital strategy. The operations have shifted from pure data deliveries to providing an HPC cluster (High-Performance Computing) where researchers can apply their code directly to the data. The lab has contributed greatly to the open-source community through models such as "KB-BERT", which have become the industry standard for processing Swedish text.

KBLab has digitized and released massive datasets (newspapers, books, radio), leading to the creation of KB-BERT and KBLab’s Whisper, which are now industry standards for Swedish NLP. These models have been downloaded hundreds of thousands of times, enabling private and public sectors to automate text analysis and transcription with high precision. Quantitative metrics for impact include model download counts (Hugging Face), GPU-cluster utilization, and the volume of petabytes processed. Qualitative tracking involves monitoring peer-reviewed citations and the integration of KBLab.

items.title: Italy AI Law 132/2025
items.category: Regulations, guidelines and standards
items.body:
Italy's first comprehensive national AI law, entered into force 10 October 2025, establishing governance, sector-specific rules, and fundamental principles for AI use, and authorising up to EUR 1B in state-backed venture capital for AI, cybersecurity and telecommunications companies.

Law No. 132 of 23 September 2025 (Gazzetta Ufficiale n. 224 of 25 September 2025), in force since 10 October 2025, makes Italy the first EU Member State to adopt a dedicated national AI framework aligned with the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689). Structured across six chapters and 28 articles, it establishes core principles—transparency, proportionality, security, data protection, accountability, gender equality, and non-discrimination—anchored in an anthropocentric approach preserving human oversight. It introduces sector-specific rules whereby AI may support but not replace decision-making in healthcare (with mandatory patient disclosure), justice, and regulated professions, while enabling its use in scientific research on anonymised data and requiring transparency toward workers, alongside the creation of a workplace AI Observatory. Governance assigns the Agency for Digital Italy (AgID) as notifying authority and the National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN) as market surveillance authority, with financial regulators retaining sectoral oversight.

items.title: IT4LIA AI Factory
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
A national AI Factory (EuroHPC selected) centred on Italy’s LEONARDO/LISA supercomputers and national AI infrastructure to provide free/discounted access and services to researchers, SMEs, startups and public administrations.

IT4LIA is a consortium-based AI Factory offering access to high-performance compute, data services, training, toolchains and domain support. Funded by the Ministry of University and Research and national partners (co-funding from EuroHPC/European Commission), IT4LIA aims to provide a one-stop shop for experimentation, model development, secure compute and training, with no-cost access routes for eligible startups, SMEs and public bodies. It supports sector pilots (agri-food, manufacturing, earth sciences, health) and runs modular training and skills programmes.

items.title: Fondo di Garanzia PMI
items.original_name: Fondo di Garanzia per le PMI
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.document_name: Fondo di Garanzia per le PMI
items.body:
Italy's central public loan guarantee fund providing state-backed guarantees of up to 80% on bank loans to SMEs and innovative startups, directly facilitating AI and technology investment finance without requiring collateral.

The Fondo Centrale di Garanzia per le PMI (FGPMI) has been operational since 2000 under Law 662/1996 and is administered by MIMIT through the fund manager Mediocredito Centrale. It provides public guarantees to banks on loans to SMEs and innovative startups, reducing lenders' credit risk and enabling businesses that would otherwise lack sufficient collateral to access finance. For innovative startups and certified incubators, the guarantee is free, priority-processed, and covers up to 80% of the loan (maximum guaranteed amount: EUR 5M per company; simplified assessment with no additional credit evaluation beyond the bank's own). For standard SME investment operations (including AI and 4.0 technology purchases), the guarantee is also 80% (maintained under Budget Law 2025 and extended through 2026 under Budget Law 2026). For liquidity operations, the guarantee was reduced to 50% from 2025. The fund can also be used to secure Nuova Sabatini loans. An extension to mid-cap companies (up to 499 employees) was approved, subject to EU authorisation. Between 2013 and 2023, the fund managed 18,053 operations for innovative startups, mobilising approximately EUR 3.4B in financing. For innovative PMEs (PMI innovative), access is free but subject to minimum creditworthiness thresholds. Total financing mobilised across all SME operations exceeds EUR 3.8B for startup/innovative SME categories alone.

items.title: EU Apply AI Strategy
items.category: AI Policy Frameworks and Initiatives (intergovernmental or supranational)
items.body:
An EU-wide strategy launched October 2025 to accelerate AI adoption across 11 key industrial and public sectors, with a specific focus on lowering barriers for SMEs through coordination, funding mechanisms, and an 'AI-first' policy culture.

The Apply AI Strategy represents the European Commission's most targeted effort to move the EU from AI development to AI deployment, with a particular emphasis on ensuring that SMEs and public sector organisations can benefit from AI. The Strategy identifies 11 priority sectors for AI integration, including healthcare, manufacturing, mobility, agriculture, energy, and public administration, and promotes an 'AI-first' organisational culture in which decision-makers are expected to consider AI as a default option when designing services and operational processes. For SMEs specifically, the Strategy connects with a broad support infrastructure: the European Digital Innovation Hubs (EDIHs) network, which provides test-before-invest facilities, digital maturity assessments, and access to expertise; the InvestAI initiative (EUR 200 billion total target investment); the Digital Europe Programme (EUR 1.3 billion allocated for AI and digital skills, 2025–2027); and the AI Factories network, which gives SMEs access to high-performance computing resources. The Strategy is coordinated through the Apply AI Alliance, a multi-stakeholder forum bringing together AI providers, industry associations, academia, social partners, and civil society. France, Germany, and Italy, as G7 members, are key implementers of the Strategy, and each has developed national-level measures aligned with it.

items.title: Canadian AI Safety Institute (CAISI Canada)
items.category: National – AI governance bodies or mechanisms
items.body:
Canada's national AI safety body established to evaluate advanced AI models for safety risks, develop safety testing methodologies, and contribute to international AI safety coordination through the Bletchley Declaration process and the International Network of AI Safety Institutes.

Announced in November 2024, the Canadian AI Safety Institute (CAISI Canada) is Canada's domestic counterpart to equivalent bodies established in the UK, the United States, Japan, and other countries participating in the Hiroshima AI Process. Operating within Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED), it focuses on three core activities: technical evaluation of advanced AI models to identify and characterise safety risks; development of safety testing methodologies and benchmarks; and international coordination through the International Network of AI Safety Institutes (INAIS). CAISI Canada contributes Canadian expertise and perspectives to the global AI safety research agenda, including work on frontier model evaluations, systemic risk assessment, and the development of safety standards. It plays a bridging role between the Canadian government, AI research institutions (including Mila, the Vector Institute, and Amii), and international partners, ensuring that Canadian AI safety research informs both domestic AI governance frameworks and international norms. The Institute was established in direct response to commitments made by Canada at the Bletchley Park AI Safety Summit in November 2023, and formalises Canada's participation in the international AI safety evaluation network.

items.title: AI-Specific Evaluation Framework for Public Procurement in Korea
items.original_name: 공공조달 AI 적용 제품·서비스 특화 심사기준 마련
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.document_name: 공공조달 AI 적용 제품·서비스 특화 심사기준 마련
items.body:
Korea’s Public Procurement Service is developing an AI-specific evaluation framework for public procurement to enable the safe and effective adoption of AI products and services. The initiative introduces new assessment criteria covering AI performance, reliability, transparency, and risk management, addressing the limitations of traditional procurement standards. It aims to support trustworthy AI adoption while fostering innovation and market access for AI suppliers.

Public procurement plays a strategic role in Korea’s AI ecosystem, representing a large-scale demand-side policy instrument. At the same time, Korea became the first country in the world to enact a comprehensive AI Basic Act, establishing overarching principles for trustworthy and responsible AI. However, despite this landmark legislation, clear operational definitions and classification criteria for AI-enabled products and services have remained underdeveloped in the procurement context. Existing public procurement evaluation systems—designed primarily for conventional goods and services—have therefore proven inadequate for assessing AI-enabled offerings, particularly with respect to algorithmic performance, data dependency, model reliability, and potential risks.

This initiative responds to that institutional and practical gap by developing an AI-specific evaluation framework tailored to public procurement. Rather than applying a single, uniform assessment model, the framework introduces procurement-instrument–specific AI evaluation approaches across major programmes, including innovation procurement, excellent product designation, and multi-supplier framework contracts. Each procurement scheme incorporates AI-relevant evaluation criteria aligned with its policy objectives and operational characteristics, recognising that AI products require different assessment logics depending on the purchasing mechanism. Instead of relying solely on legal definitions, the framework provides practical and evaluative criteria to identify and assess AI-enabled products and services within procurement processes. New assessment dimensions include AI model appropriateness, robustness, transparency, lifecycle risk management, and alignment with public sector use cases, complementing existing criteria on public value, performance, and innovation. This approach allows contracting authorities to more accurately distinguish genuinely AI-enabled solutions from conventional products, while ensuring that AI-specific risks are systematically considered.

items.title: AI verkstaden - AI node for public administration
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
The "AI-verkstaden" is a national initiative that provides public sector organisations with shared, secure environments and ready‑to‑use AI services to help them develop, test, and use AI solutions. It is designed to support government agencies, regions, and municipalities by offering technical tools, guidance, and trustworthy AI services. The initiative was developed to address common challenges such as limited AI competence and  legal uncertainty.

AI‑verkstaden is a national initiative designed to help Sweden’s public sector adopt artificial intelligence safely, efficiently and at scale. It responds to long‑standing challenges across agencies, regions and municipalities, including fragmented digital infrastructure, uneven AI competence, inconsistent data quality, legal uncertainty and unequal access to technical resources. Many smaller public organisations in particular lack the environments, support and guidance needed to use AI responsibly. Against this backdrop, AI‑verkstaden leverages rapid technological progress and Sweden’s growing need for digital sovereignty, secure data management and a coordinated approach to technology adoption.

The initiative’s core objective is to provide a shared, secure national infrastructure where public actors can experiment with, develop and deploy AI solutions. This includes lab, development and production environments; a catalogue of quality‑assured AI services; and structured support that ranges from self‑service resources to expert legal, technical and change‑management advice. By enabling public actors to share models, align standards and coordinate legal and technical assessments, AI‑verkstaden reduces redundant work and promotes more coherent, efficient and trustworthy AI use across the public sector. Its broader aim is to raise AI maturity, improve service quality and strengthen Sweden’s digital resilience and civil preparedness. AI‑verkstaden is being established over multiple years (2026–2030), gradually expanding its service catalogue, infrastructure and user base. It will move from pilots and foundational support functions toward full operational capacity using a hybrid model that combines a state‑controlled “community cloud” with approved private‑sector resources. Over time, it will be institutionalised through stable governance shared between the two government agencies responsible for its oversight. Its flexible architecture ensures it can adapt to evolving technologies, regulatory requirements and user needs.

Early experimentation has already demonstrated value. A pilot with the Mörbylånga municipality tested an AI service for masking personal data, showing that local actors can securely access and use AI within a governed environment. The pilot validated technical, legal and contractual processes and highlighted user support needs, helping refine requirements for future scaling. Early user feedback confirmed that the service lowered adoption barriers. These results were assessed through real‑world testing in operational settings.

items.title: AI Sovereign Compute Infrastructure Program (AI SCIP) / Canadian Sovereign AI Compute Strategy
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
Canada's flagship sovereign AI infrastructure investment, comprising three complementary streams: a CAD 705M public supercomputing facility (AI SCIP), up to CAD 700M for private-sector AI data centres (AI Compute Challenge), and CAD 200M in near-term augmentation of existing public compute infrastructure.

Announced as part of Canada's Budget 2024 investment of CAD 2 billion over five years (2024–25 to 2028–29) to secure Canada's AI advantage, the Canadian Sovereign AI Compute Strategy was formally launched in December 2024. It is organised into three pillars: (1) AI Sovereign Compute Infrastructure Program (AI SCIP) — up to CAD 705M to build a state-of-the-art, publicly-owned, Canadian-operated AI supercomputing system; ISED issued a call for Statements of Interest in February 2025 (closed May 2025), with eligible proponents including not-for-profits, for-profits, academic institutions, and consortia; (2) AI Compute Challenge — up to CAD 700M through a competitive call for proposals to support private-sector AI data centres offering affordable compute to Canadian businesses, with a focus on data sovereignty, sustainability, and use of Canadian supply chains; and (3) Near-term augmentation — CAD 200M to immediately expand existing public compute infrastructure, including CAD 85M to the Digital Research Alliance of Canada, CAD 60M to AI Institutes, and CAD 30M for the VITAL health AI infrastructure. Separately, ISED also launched in January 2026 a non-competitive intake for large-scale sovereign AI data centres (100MW+). The AI SCIP facility will be led by Shared Services Canada (SSC) and the National Research Council of Canada (NRC) for government and industry R&D, including for national security. The broader strategy aims to make Canada a globally competitive location for AI research, reduce reliance on foreign cloud infrastructure, ensure Canadian data sovereignty, and support academic, government, and commercial AI workloads.

items.title: Vendor Innovation Program (VIP) - Canada Health Infoway
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
Funding programme supporting development and implementation of digital health technologies including AI tools.

Canada Health Infoway’s VIP provides targeted funding and partnership support to technology vendors (including SMEs) to develop, test and implement interoperable digital health innovations aligned with the Pan-Canadian Interoperability Roadmap. Funded projects include AI-assisted diagnostics, decision support tools and data-standards projects; the programme emphasises clinical validation and integration into health provider networks. The VIP seeks to de-risk pilots, enable evaluation in real healthcare settings, and scale solutions that improve care and system performance.

items.title: UK National Data Library (NDL)
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
The UK National Data Library (NDL) is a government initiative to create a central infrastructure for the responsible management and sharing of public sector data, enabling businesses, researchers and public servants to access high-value datasets to deliver better public services, drive economic growth and support AI innovation.

The National Data Library was announced as part of the UK Government's AI Opportunities Action Plan in January 2025, based on recommendations from entrepreneur and AI advisor Matt Clifford. Its creation is overseen by DSIT, with close involvement from the Government Digital Service (GDS). The NDL completed an extensive discovery phase in 2025, including public attitudes research, consultation with over 200 organisations and expert bodies (including the Open Data Institute, Wellcome Trust, Public Digital, The Tony Blair Institute and The Startup Coalition), and five 'kickstarter' projects designed to test approaches to systemic data reform. An architecture design contract of £650,000 was awarded to esynergy in November 2025 to produce a federated architecture blueprint for the NDL. The NDL's design principles prioritise: (1) public benefit and ethical data use; (2) data security and privacy safeguards; (3) a federated model that does not centralise data but provides shared infrastructure for access; (4) AI-readiness, with guidelines for making government datasets AI-ready published by GDS; and (5) public trust through ongoing citizen engagement. Economic analyses suggest a fully developed AI-ready data ecosystem underpinned by the NDL could generate £40 billion annually in productivity gains by 2030.

items.title: UK AI for Science Strategy
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
A national strategy designed to accelerate the application of artificial intelligence across scientific research and discovery in the United Kingdom.

The AI for Science Strategy was published by the UK government to accelerate the integration of artificial intelligence into scientific discovery and innovation. The strategy seeks to position the United Kingdom as a global leader in AI-enabled research by investing in infrastructure, data resources and interdisciplinary collaborations. It focuses on enabling scientists to use advanced AI systems to analyse complex datasets, simulate natural phenomena and accelerate breakthroughs in fields such as life sciences, materials science, climate research and energy. The strategy promotes the creation of mission-driven research programmes where AI techniques are applied to large-scale scientific challenges, while also strengthening the computing infrastructure required to train and run advanced models. It encourages collaboration between universities, national laboratories, startups and established industry actors. In addition, the strategy emphasises responsible innovation, skills development and access to shared data resources.

items.title: TiNAI (Tamil Nadu Land Use Information System) (Subnational: Tamil Nadu State)
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
TiNAI (Tamil Nadu Land Use Information System) is an AI-enabled geospatial and Digital Twin platform designed to support evidence-based land-use planning. It uses artificial intelligence to analyse multi-sector data and generate clear insights that help policymakers understand climate, urban, and environmental challenges. The platform was created to address fragmented data and improve coordinated, transparent decision-making across sectors.

TiNAI (Tamil Nadu Land Use Information System) was developed to address a persistent research–policy disconnect in land-use governance. Although large volumes of spatial, environmental, and sectoral data existed across departments, they remained fragmented, limiting cross-sector interpretation and evidence-based planning. TiNAI responds to this challenge by integrating multi-sector datasets into a unified geospatial Digital Twin platform supported by artificial intelligence, enabling holistic analysis of land, climate, water, energy, agriculture, forests, disaster risks, and urban systems.

The initiative aims to strengthen scientific decision-making by transforming complex spatial datasets into interpretable insights for policymakers. Through AI-assisted pattern analysis, KPI synthesis, and scenario exploration, the platform supports fiscal planning, resource optimisation, environmental sustainability, and climate resilience. TiNAI includes thematic modules such as Land Use and Land Cover (LULC), climate indicators (temperature trends, rainfall, heat stress), forest monitoring, renewable energy suitability (solar and wind potential), disaster risk (landslides, forest fires), coastal vulnerability, agriculture trends, water resource analytics, and urban growth dynamics. These modules are accessible through interactive maps, dashboards, and analytical tools that enable multi-dimensional assessment.

Since its initial development as a land-use information system, TiNAI has evolved into an integrated AI-enabled spatial intelligence and Digital Twin architecture. The platform has progressively expanded its modules, analytical tools, and key performance indicators, while strengthening interdepartmental data integration. Its adoption in planning workflows demonstrates its role in supporting fiscal allocation and identifying strategic development opportunities. Looking ahead, TiNAI is expected to institutionalise cross-sector data integration further by incorporating health, housing, municipal, and additional statistical datasets. This expansion will enhance monitoring of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), disaster risk reduction frameworks, and climate resilience metrics. With an open, scalable architecture, the platform has potential for replication across other states or regions seeking integrated, AI-driven land and resource governance systems.

items.title: Skills Bootcamps (AI & Digital)
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
Free, flexible training courses of up to 16 weeks co-designed with employers, enabling adults to rapidly gain in-demand digital and AI skills, with a guaranteed job interview on completion.

Launched from Autumn 2020 as part of the UK Government's Lifetime Skills Guarantee and National Skills Fund, Skills Bootcamps are delivered across England by training providers, further education colleges, and employers in partnership with local areas. They are funded by the Department for Education (DfE) and, from 2025–26, directly through Mayoral Strategic Authorities and other local areas. The programme covers a wide range of sectors including digital (coding, cybersecurity, data analytics, AI, software development), green, construction, engineering, health and care, and HGV driving. Bootcamps offer training at Levels 3–5 (and Level 2 in some sectors), delivered online, face-to-face, or blended, and typically last up to 16 weeks.
