Learners must be 19 or over; the programme targets employed adults, self-employed, unemployed, and those returning to work or transitioning careers. Co-funding is required from employers for employed learners (typically 10% for SMEs, 30% for large employers). On completion, participants are guaranteed a job interview with a participating employer. In 2022–23, the DfE committed GBP 150M for Wave 3 alone. By 2024, the programme had supported hundreds of thousands of learners across England with AI and digital skills among the highest-demand areas. The programme is being progressively devolved to mayoral combined authorities and local areas from 2025–26.

items.title: Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Credit
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
Canada's largest federal R&D tax incentive programme, providing investment tax credits (ITCs) to businesses conducting eligible scientific research and experimental development in Canada, including AI system development, with enhanced refundable rates for qualifying small Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs).

Canada’s Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) program, administered by the Canada Revenue Agency, is a tax-based incentive that supports businesses conducting research and development in Canada by allowing them to claim a portion of eligible R&D costs through their corporate tax filings. Companies receive either a 35% fully refundable credit on up to CAD 6 million in annual qualifying expenditures (primarily for Canadian-controlled private corporations and, more recently, certain public firms) or a 15% partially refundable credit for other businesses. Eligible activities include experimental development, applied and basic research, and supporting work such as software engineering and AI development, provided it involves genuine technical uncertainty and systematic experimentation. Recent updates have expanded eligibility to include capital expenditures like equipment, raised thresholds so more mid-sized firms can access enhanced rates, and introduced faster, AI-assisted claim processing. In addition to the federal incentive, most provinces offer supplementary credits, allowing companies to recover a significant share of their R&D investment.

items.title: Scale AI Supercluster (Supply Chains and Logistics Excellence AI)
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
Canada's national AI-powered supply chain Global Innovation Cluster, providing co-investment grants to industry consortia developing and adopting AI solutions across supply chain sectors, headquartered in Montréal.

Originally selected in February 2018 as one of five Innovation Superclusters under the Innovation Superclusters Initiative (ISI), Scale AI is an independent, industry-led not-for-profit funded by ISED. It operates under the Global Innovation Clusters (GIC) programme (renamed from ISI in 2022), which received an additional CAD 750M in Budget 2022 for the clusters collectively, plus CAD 125M from the second phase of the Pan-Canadian AI Strategy (2022) to accelerate AI commercialisation. Scale AI's total federal funding envelope is approximately CAD 284M over the programme period. Scale AI funds two categories of projects: (1) Industry-led collaborative projects for AI adoption in supply chains — companies can access up to 40% of eligible costs (up to 50% for projects in Québec), with no prescribed minimum or maximum per project; projects must have a minimum budget of CAD 1M and must involve at least one Canadian SME; and (2) Workforce training grants — refunding up to 85% of eligible costs for AI and digital intelligence training programmes designed by businesses. Eligible sectors include supply chain operators and AI solutions providers in retail, manufacturing, transportation, logistics, ICT, and critical infrastructure. Scale AI has funded hundreds of projects across Canada and has attracted over 8,000 members and 2,465+ project partners, with CAD 2.37B+ co-invested with industry across the five clusters since 2018.

items.title: Regional Artificial Intelligence Initiative (RAII)
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
A multi-regional funding programme that supports AI commercialization and adoption projects by businesses across Canada.

Announced in Budget 2024, RAII channels funding through Canada’s regional development agencies to support projects across regions that productise AI, help SMEs adopt AI responsibly, and grow regional AI clusters. Pillars include adoption support, commercialisation, and ecosystem development (grants, repayable financing or non-repayable contributions depending on the delivery agency). It aims to accelerate SME adoption, foster partnerships between industry and researchers, and create regional demonstration projects and pilots.

items.title: Public Procurement Directive No. 44/2026 for Data Science and Artificial Intelligence Projects
items.original_name: Directiva de Contratación Pública N°44/2026 para la adquisición de proyectos que incorporen ciencia de datos e inteligencia artificial
items.category: Regulations, guidelines and standards
items.document_name: Directiva de Contratación Pública N°44/2026 para la adquisición de proyectos que incorporen ciencia de datos e inteligencia artificial
items.body:
ChileCompra published Public Procurement Directive No. 44/2026, which provides recommendations to public sector entities for procuring data science and artificial intelligence projects through Mercado Público. In March 2026, the 2023 version was updated, taking into account the reform to Law No. 19,886 and its new regulation. Its objective is to guide the responsible, ethical, and secure use of data and AI systems in public procurement.

ChileCompra’s Public Procurement Directive No. 44/2026 provides guidance to public entities incorporating data analytics and artificial intelligence (AI) into their procurement processes, updating and expanding the guidance first issued in 2023 under the Ethical Algorithms project led by Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez, in which ChileCompra participates. The update responds to changes introduced by the modernization of the Public Procurement Law and its new regulation, with a focus on maximizing the public value of these technologies while safeguarding legality, ethics, and information security. 

The directive applies to all procurement modalities, with particular emphasis on projects involving personal data processing, high technological complexity, or automated decision-making. It identifies common risks—such as lack of algorithmic transparency, bias in AI models, and cybersecurity vulnerabilities—and establishes recommendations to mitigate them, including rigorous planning, the formation of multidisciplinary teams, and prior ethical, legal, and technical assessments before initiating the procurement process. 

It also proposes specific contractual clauses, such as algorithmic audits, data protection impact assessments, and information security measures. These aim to ensure standards of transparency, fairness, and accountability throughout the project lifecycle, from design and award to operation and closure. 

A cross-cutting principle is explainability: decisions derived from the use of AI must be understandable and explainable to people, strengthening public trust and enabling oversight and continuous improvement. Through these guidelines, the directive supports effective planning and procurement of data and AI projects, enhancing their positive impact on public management and on the design of more efficient and inclusive public policies.

Given its recent publication (March 12, 2026), results are primarily expected: improved quality and consistency in AI-related tender documents, reduced risks of bias and opacity, and enhanced data security and governance. An increase in algorithmic audits, data protection impact assessments, and explainability clauses in contracts is anticipated. The expected impact is a more responsible and trustworthy adoption of AI in government, leading to better services and greater public trust.

items.title: PresidencIA: Generative AI Adoption Programme for the Spanish Prime Minister’s Office
items.original_name: PresidencIA: Programa de Adopción de IA Generativa para el Gabinete de Presidencia del Gobierno de España
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.document_name: PresidencIA: Programa de Adopción de IA Generativa para el Gabinete de Presidencia del Gobierno de España
items.body:
Leveraging on 3 pillars (Community, Applications and Infrastructure), PresidencIA builds AI literacy among staff through workshops, community and best practices, develops custom AI tools for processes in the PM’s Office, and pursues on-premises AI infrastructure for tech sovereignty. It also works to position Spain as a partner for leading AI labs on safety and alignment. The programme addresses the gap between AI’s potential and practical government capacity.

PresidencIA is a comprehensive programme designed to accelerate the responsible adoption of generative AI within the Spanish Prime Minister’s Office (Gabinete de Presidencia). While AI offers significant potential to improve public‑sector decision‑making and service delivery, many administrations lack the internal capacity, tools and infrastructure needed to adopt it safely. PresidencIA responds by combining skills development, purpose‑built applications, sovereign infrastructure and international engagement into a single, integrated approach.

The programme’s first pillar focuses on community and capacity building. Through hands‑on workshops such as Whispering to AIs, Prototyping with AI and Researching with AI, several hundred public servants have developed practical skills in prompt engineering and responsible AI use. These activities prioritise experimentation and peer learning over theoretical instruction, supported by an active community of practice where staff share experiences and best practices. 
The second pillar delivers AI applications tailored to the Prime Minister’s Office. These include ServetIA, a research platform that produces source‑verified analytical outputs to support policy work; CiudadanIA, which automates the summarisation of citizen correspondence addressed to the President, reducing processing time and improving response quality; and GlobalAlert, which provides real‑time geopolitical monitoring and threat analysis. The programme also developed PromptAventura, a gamified AI literacy tool now validated and transferred to the government intranet. In addition, PresidencIA produced open‑source components, including an LLM evaluation workbench used to test prompts and models at scale through LLM‑as‑a‑judge methodologies.

The infrastructure pillar addresses AI sovereignty and secure deployment. PresidencIA has tested open‑weight language models for on‑premises use, enabling sensitive data processing without reliance on external cloud providers. In collaboration with the government IT unit (U.TIC), the programme is assessing the feasibility of a dedicated internal AI compute cluster and fine‑tuning models for specific government use cases. Alongside domestic infrastructure, PresidencIA also pursues international engagement, positioning Spain as a strategic partner for leading AI labs and fostering collaboration on alignment, safety research and responsible deployment of frontier AI systems in government contexts.

items.title: Patent Box
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
A UK tax incentive allowing companies to elect a reduced 10% corporation tax rate on profits derived from qualifying patented inventions, including AI-enabled products and processes, to encourage the commercialisation and retention of intellectual property in the UK.

Introduced on 1 April 2013 and fully phased in by 1 April 2017, the Patent Box regime is administered by HMRC under Part 8A of the Corporation Tax Act 2010. It allows qualifying UK companies to apply a 10% corporation tax rate (compared to the standard 25% rate) on profits attributable to qualifying intellectual property income, including income from patents granted by the UK Intellectual Property Office, the European Patent Office, or the national patent offices of certain EEA states. Eligibility requires the company to be subject to UK corporation tax, to own or hold an exclusive licence for a qualifying patent, and to have undertaken qualifying development (i.e. made a significant technical contribution). The OECD nexus approach applies: relief is proportional to the fraction of R&D carried out by the company itself. The regime applies to patent-related income from sales of patented products (even if only one component is patented), licence royalties, damages from infringement, and process-linked profits. AI companies can benefit when their systems, algorithms, or processes incorporate patentable technical inventions. Software patents qualify where they cover a technical improvement to a product or process (not mere software as such). The Patent Box is typically used alongside the R&D tax credit regime (merged RDEC/ERIS). According to HMRC, the manufacturing sector accounts for over 60% of claimants by number and the majority of relief claimed. In 2022–23, approximately 1,600 companies claimed, yielding £1.47B in tax relief. HMRC published updated compliance guidance (GfC9) in November 2024 requiring more detailed Patent Box computations.

items.title: PALOMA: Artificial Intelligence for Early Detection of Unwanted Loneliness in Older Adults (Subnational: Madrid)
items.original_name: PALOMA: Inteligencia Artificial para la Detección Temprana de la Soledad No Deseada en Personas Mayores
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.document_name: PALOMA: Inteligencia Artificial para la Detección Temprana de la Soledad No Deseada en Personas Mayores
items.body:
PALOMA is an artificial intelligence system that makes phone calls to people over 75 who live alone to detect situations of unwanted loneliness. It conducts short conversations with a natural sounding voice, identifies risk signals, and offers information or municipal follow up. The project helps reach more people, detect needs earlier, and connect them quickly with social support.

Unwanted loneliness affects older adults over 75 who live alone in Madrid and can lead to isolation, declining health, and loss of autonomy. Early detection is difficult, as many do not seek help and traditional channels—postal mail or in person visits—are not sufficient to identify those who may be at risk. To address this challenge, the Madrid City Council launched a pilot initiative using artificial intelligence to proactively contact this population group and better understand their situation through brief telephone conversations. 
PALOMA uses natural language processing technology capable of maintaining conversations with a natural sounding synthetic voice and administering a short questionnaire designed by social services professionals. The AI analyzes responses to detect signs of loneliness, classify risk levels, and offer follow up calls or information about municipal services. Cases flagged as relevant are always reviewed by professional staff, ensuring safe, ethical, and tailored intervention. This combination of AI and human oversight expands municipal capacity without replacing the professional role, aligning with principles of trustworthy and human centred AI.

The project has three main goals: improving early detection of unwanted loneliness, enabling more personalized interventions, and increasing access to activities and support services. It also modernizes the relationship between citizens and the administration, showing how AI can support social services in an efficient, accessible, and respectful way. Automated calls make it possible to reach thousands of people quickly and at a cost far lower than traditional alternatives such as call centers, significantly increasing the reach and effectiveness of social policies.

PALOMA carried out 5,163 calls, completed 2,071 conversations, and enabled 646 people to request municipal follow up. Of these, 602 were referred to social programs and 236 accepted a home visit; 84% showed signs of loneliness. The system identified 44 clear high risk cases and reached individuals who would not have contacted the city through other means. AI expanded reach, accelerated detection, and optimized resources. Results were measured through call analysis, conversion rates, referrals, and professional follow up.

A key strength of PALOMA is its capacity to scale. Traditional outreach programmes are limited by staff time, whereas AI enabled calling can reach thousands of people quickly and at low cost. The pilot contacted 5,000 people in only two weeks, leading to 646 individuals requesting follow up and enabling targeted support for those experiencing loneliness. These results demonstrate the potential for broader deployment and for replication in other municipalities facing similar demographic challenges.

items.title: Messina Urban Digital Twin (GDU) – AI-enabled Urban Intelligence Platform (Subnational: Municipality of Messina)
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
The Messina Urban Digital Twin (GDU) is an AI-enabled platform that integrates data from IoT sensors, administrative sources and urban systems to support decision-making and scenario simulation. It transforms fragmented urban data into a dynamic and interactive model of the city. The initiative aims to improve planning, resource management and public services through data-driven insights.

The Messina Urban Digital Twin (GDU) was developed to address the fragmentation of urban data across multiple systems and the lack of integrated tools for evidence-based decision-making in local government. Cities generate large volumes of data through IoT sensors, administrative processes and external systems, but these data are often siloed and underutilised.

The initiative integrates heterogeneous data sources, including IoT infrastructure, environmental monitoring, mobility systems and administrative datasets, into a unified digital representation of the urban environment. AI techniques are used to analyse data patterns, support predictive insights and enable simulation of complex urban scenarios, such as traffic flows, environmental impacts and resource allocation. The system enables public officials to explore “what-if” scenarios and supports strategic planning, operational management and policy evaluation. It is designed as a modular and scalable architecture, allowing progressive integration of new data sources and services.

The initiative is part of the broader investment framework of the PN METRO Plus 2021–2027 programme, ensuring alignment with national and European urban innovation priorities and supporting its long-term sustainability and scalability. The GDU is also aligned with national and European digital strategies and integrates with the municipality’s Open Data ecosystem, promoting transparency and enabling future reuse by developers, researchers and other public administrations.

items.title: Merged R&D Tax Relief / ERIS (UK)
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
A unified UK corporation tax relief scheme replacing the previous SME and RDEC regimes, providing a 20% above-the-line expenditure credit for all companies, with an enhanced 27% payable credit for R&D-intensive loss-making SMEs (ERIS).

The UK’s R&D tax relief system, administered by HM Revenue & Customs, was restructured in April 2024 into a single unified scheme known as the Merged RDEC, which applies to companies of all sizes and sectors. Under this regime, businesses receive a headline 20% “above-the-line” tax credit on qualifying R&D expenditure—covering costs such as staffing, software, cloud computing, data, consumables, and certain subcontracted activities—but because the credit is treated as taxable income, the effective net benefit is typically around 15–16% after tax. A complementary programme, Enhanced R&D Intensive Support (ERIS), targets loss-making small and medium-sized enterprises whose R&D spending exceeds 30% of total costs, offering a more generous combination of enhanced deductions and payable credits that can raise the effective benefit to roughly 27%. Recent updates have also tightened rules around overseas R&D activity and introduced clearer compliance guidance, aiming to simplify the system while focusing support on genuinely innovation-driven companies.

items.title: MencIA: Sovereign AI Strategy for Territorial Cohesion. (Subnational: Lugo)
items.original_name: MencIA: Estrategia de IA soberana para la cohesión territorial
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.document_name: MencIA: Estrategia de IA soberana para la cohesión territorial
items.body:
MencIA is a sovereign AI strategy that aims to offer a Platform as a Service (PaaS) to 66 municipalities in the province of Lugo with fewer than 20,000 inhabitants. It will enable local councils to adopt secure, local, open-source AI tools, avoiding dependence on large corporations. The initiative will bridge the digital divide, ensuring that small towns benefit from AI through publicly controlled technology, privacy by design, and efficiency.

MencIA addresses the dilemma of “Digital Feudalism,” where public administrations cede control of data to proprietary “black box” technologies. Instead, this strategy proposes a new path: realistic technological sovereignty based on open-source AI models running on the Lugo Provincial Council's own servers.

The approach chosen by MencIA allows it to comply with its three key rules: 
Privacy and security, as data never leaves the perimeter of our servers.Adaptability, as by using AI models installed on our servers, we can design and adapt the tools we create to our needs. Economic sustainability, as the model allows us to save on recurring licensing costs and invest in talent.The guiding principle of the model is “AI as Co-Pilot.” We defend the idea of an augmented administration in which AI never replaces public employees, but rather enhances their capabilities. Human oversight is non-negotiable for any administrative act with legal consequences. The architecture uses tools such as Ollama, vLLM, Docker, LangChain, and OpenWebUI to configure a dual system of specialized AI assistants and applications that solve specific problems with a minimal learning curve for use. MencIA natively integrates the principles of privacy, cybersecurity, and governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) into its design. The native integration of all these elements facilitates compliance with the European AI Act and the GDPR, as well as all our national regulations on AI and data protection. A key pillar of the model is “Green in AI” sustainability. By using Small Language Models (SLMs) and a “3-click” interaction design, the strategy minimizes token generation and energy consumption, demonstrating that high-performance AI can be environmentally responsible. MencIA serves as a scalable model for territorialcohesion in the European context and aligns with other Spanish and European AI implementation initiatives such as the Spanish Government's ALIA project, the OpenEuroLLM project, and the European Union's Apply AI strategy.

items.title: Innovative Solutions Canada (ISC)
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
A federal innovation procurement programme that challenges Canadian SMEs to develop pre-commercial AI solutions for real government needs, funding proof-of-concept and prototype development, with a pathway to government commercialisation contracts of up to CAD 8M.

Launched in 2018 (merging the former Build in Canada Innovation Program and ISC predecessor programmes) and administered by ISED, Innovative Solutions Canada uses the federal government's buying power as a first purchaser of pre-commercial Canadian technology. The programme operates through two streams: (1) Challenge Stream — government departments and agencies post real operational challenges (including AI challenges for workflow automation, decision support, and process improvement); eligible Canadian SMEs with fewer than 500 FTE employees apply and can receive up to CAD 150,000 for a Phase 1 proof-of-feasibility (up to 6 months) and up to CAD 1M for Phase 2 prototype development (up to 2 years); and (2) Testing Stream — departments post solicitations for late-stage pre-commercial prototypes for operational testing; successful innovators receive contracts for testing in live government environments. Upon successful testing or prototype completion, eligible SMEs access the Pathway to Commercialization, enabling non-competitive government procurement contracts of up to CAD 8M per contract over three years. As of 2024, ISC had awarded over 960 contracts worth over CAD 446M across both streams. ISED's AI-specific challenge solicitation (EN578-25ISC2) targets AI and robotic process automation (RPA) solutions for government servic delivery. The programme is aligned with the Government of Canada's AI Strategy for the Federal Public Service and Treasury Board Secretariat (TBS) digital procurement policy.

items.title: IPS Córdoba Assistant — AI Policy Analysis Agent for Social Progress Governance (Subnational: Province of Córdoba)
items.original_name: Asistente IPS Córdoba: agente de análisis de políticas de IA para la gobernanza del progreso social.
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.document_name: Asistente IPS Córdoba: agente de análisis de políticas de IA para la gobernanza del progreso social.
items.body:
The IPS Córdoba Agent is an AI-powered policy tool integrated into the Social Progress Index dashboard for Córdoba’s 427 localities. It analyses quality-of-life data across 12 components and 57 indicators, combining social metrics, trends, and policy literature. More than a chatbot, it provides contextualised analysis and actionable recommendations so mayors and local officials can turn data into informed public policy, targeted investment, and evidence-based decisions.

The Province of Córdoba measures the Social Progress Index across all 427 of its localities over two census periods, producing one of the most granular subnational quality-of-life datasets in Latin America. Despite the richness of this data, a persistent and well-documented gap existed between data production and data use in public administration: mayors, municipal officials, and local planners often lacked the time, technical capacity, or analytical tools to translate 57 social indicators into concrete policy decisions. Complex statistical products were being generated but not acted upon. The IPS Córdoba Agent was developed specifically to close this gap — not by simplifying the data, but by building an intelligent analytical layer on top of it that is capable of reasoning across indicators, localities, time periods, and policy frameworks simultaneously.

The initiative has three core objectives. First, to democratise access to complex social intelligence: any local official — regardless of technical background — should be able to query their territory's social performance in natural language and receive a rigorous, grounded analysis in return. Second, to support evidence-based policy design at the local level by connecting social diagnoses directly to actionable intervention options drawn from provincial development frameworks. Third, to strengthen a culture of data-driven governance across Córdoba's municipalities, embedding AI-assisted analysis as a routine part of local decision-making rather than an exceptional resource.

The IPS Córdoba Assistant is designed and should be understood as a policy analysis agent, not a retrieval chatbot. The distinction is substantial and consequential. A conventional chatbot answers discrete questions by retrieving pre-existing text. This agent, by contrast, performs multi-step analytical reasoning: it interprets a locality's indicator-level results, identifies patterns of improvement or deterioration across dimensions and sub-dimensions, benchmarks performance against provincial averages, infers which population groups are most affected by specific social gaps, and generates policy recommendations grounded in a curated knowledge base that includes academic literature on human development, the provincial development model, and validated intervention frameworks. The agent synthesises all of this into a coherent, contextualised policy narrative — a form of analytical output that would otherwise require a trained policy analyst.

items.title: Guideline for Japanese Government’s Procurements and Utilizations of Generative AI for the sake of Evolution and Innovation of Public Administration
items.original_name: デジタル社会推進標準ガイドライン DS-920  行政の進化と革新のための生成AIの調達・利活用に係るガイドライン
items.category: Regulations, guidelines and standards
items.document_name: デジタル社会推進標準ガイドライン DS-920  行政の進化と革新のための生成AIの調達・利活用に係るガイドライン
items.body:
"Japan's GenAI Procurement & Utilization Guideline" was formulated in 2025 to establish rules for the procurement and use of generative AI across national government. It creates an AI governance framework requiring each ministry to appoint a Chief AI Officer (CAIO), conduct risk assessments to each generative AI systems, and implement procurement based on specific check sheets. The guideline aims to accelerate adoption of generative AI in government while managing its risks.

As AI-related technologies advance rapidly, and their utilization expands across the public and private sectors, the Japanese Government recognized the necessity to establish rules and frameworks to promote the proper procurement and utilization of generative AI within its administrative operations, while ensuring appropriate risk management. Accordingly, the “Guideline for Japanese Governments’ Procurements and Utilizations of Generative AI for the sake of Evolution and Innovation of Public Administration” was approved by the Council for the Promotion of a Digital Society Executive Board on 27 May 2025.
The Guideline was developed by referring to domestic and international initiatives, including the AI Guidelines for Business, the outcomes of the Hiroshima AI Process, and discussions in frameworks such as the OECD and the G7.
The Guideline applies to the national government staff and covers text-generating AI systems, including those incorporating large language models (LLMs), used as components of government information systems, excluding systems handling classified or national security–related information.
Under the Guideline, each ministry or agency should appoint a Chief AI Officer (CAIO) responsible for promoting utilization while ensuring AI governance, risk management, and, enhance AI literacy among government staff. Based on the “Model User Rule for Generative AI” the CAIO develops rules for users within each ministry or agency.
The Guideline also establishes a government-wide Advanced AI Utilization Advisory Board to provide advice on projects likely to be classified as high-risk, share best practices, and consider revisions of the Guideline. It introduces the “High-Risk AI Project Finder” assessing risks based on factors such as users, operations, confidential information or personal data, and staff judgment on outputs. Given rapid technological advancement, the Guideline is to be reviewed and revised in a timely manner, with planned revisions from fiscal year 2026 onward, including scope expansion, enhancements to procurement check sheets, updates reflecting institutional and regulatory developments, and revisions to the High-Risk AI Project Finder.

items.title: Government Communication Service Assist
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
Assist is a secure tool created in-house to support government communicators. It went live in April 2025, following the initial prototype launch in November 2023. The tool features pre-built, task-specific prompts to save users time. It enables communicators to brainstorm ideas, produce first draft communication products and review work in a fraction of the time it would otherwise take manually.

In 2023, the Government Communication Service (GCS) identified "lack of time" as a key barrier to innovation for its 6,500-strong communications profession, with members spending large portions of their working day on routine tasks such as producing first drafts of content. 

Assist is a secure, generative AI tool built by government communicators, for government communicators. It supports users to brainstorm ideas, produce first drafts, and review work through communications-specific pre-built prompts spanning all seven GCS disciplines. Outputs are grounded in GCS policies, frameworks, and best practice guidance. Responsible use and human oversight are central to its design: Assist produces suggested drafts that communicators develop further, applying their own critical thinking and judgement. 

Assist saves the average user around three hours per week, contributing to projected annual efficiency savings of £5.5 million. More than 90% of the 6,500-strong GCS profession are now using Assist, across 210 government organisations. Over 30% of users log in each week, with both users and usage growing weekly, 98% of surveyed users find it useful in their role, and 88% report applying its outputs in their work. Finally, over 70% of all potential users have completed the bespoke 'AI for Communicators' training course, which is mandatory to gain access to the tool. After completing the course, users report a 23% improvement in confidence using AI at work.

Lessons Learned
Build for your users, not just for technology: Assist was designed around the real daily tasks of government communicators, with discipline-specific prompts shaped by user research. Relevance drives adoption.Make responsible use structural, not optional: mandatory training, ethical frameworks, and human oversight were built into the tool from the outset, not added afterwards.Scale with a people-centred approach: GCS published "The People Factor" guide and the Mitigating Hidden AI Risks Toolkit, drawing on its own rollout experience to help other organisations scale AI tools safely.Overall, government communicators spend less time on routine drafting and more time on strategic, creative, and high-impact work. By embedding GCS standards directly into its outputs, Assist also improves the consistency and quality of government communications at scale, whilst building AI capability and confidence across the profession.

items.title: GovAI Chat
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
GovAI Chat is a secure, government-controlled generative AI tool developed specifically for the Australian Public Service (APS). The goal of GovAI Chat is to give public servants access to the advanced AI capabilities of a contemporary chat interface tailored to the APS context – with the security, compliance, and public sector knowledge embedded in the GovAI environment.

GovAI Chat is a secure, government-controlled generative AI tool developed specifically for the Australian Public Service (APS). It is different from commercial tools (for example, ChatGPT or Microsoft Copilot) because it is designed to:
 
Operate within secure onshore infrastructure with vendors who are compliant with the Australian Government Hosting Certification Framework which ensures data remains securely within Australia and under government control.Meet the highest standards of security and compliance, including meeting the Australia’s Protective Security Policy Framework, enabling safe handling of sensitive and PROTECTED-level information.Offer equitable access to all APS staff, with usage costs covered during the pilot phase.Allow access to a range of AI models providing choice and flexibility and limiting the risk of vendor lock-in.Enable the APS to build digital capability, drive innovation, and maintain public trust in the responsible use of AI.
 GovAI Chat will increase the capability of the APS to deliver more for the Australian public, while maintaining standards and complying with legal frameworks for cyber security and data sovereignty. The result will be a safer and smarter way to work that supports operational integrity and delivers value through time saved and reduced rework. GovAI Chat will continue to evolve throughout Alpha and Beta trial stages based on user feedback, security requirements and technical capability. The delivery team will regularly incorporate feedback, distil insights, prioritise for future implementation and adjust the product roadmap as required. The GovAI trial will consider a range of potential enhancements and continue to seek feedback on these, considering impacts to key themes such as scale, scope, schedule, budget, usability and trust. We will embed a continuous observability and evaluation process to review all relevant metrics. Initial trials of GovAI Chat with APS staff are expected to begin in April 2026.

items.title: Fraud Risk Assessment Accelerator
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
An application that allows users to use Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPT) to generate draft Fraud Risk Assessments (FRA)s by reference to a defined set of source documents. This allows the UK's Public Sector Fraud Authority (PSFA), and external teams it collaborates with, to generate draft FRAs using Large Language Models (LLMs).

FRAs are a critical safeguard in public spending, yet their production is slow, specialist-intensive, and inconsistent across departments. This bottleneck means fraud controls are often underdeveloped at the point of implementation. The UK's experience during the COVID-19 pandemic illustrated this risk at scale: emergency schemes were exploited extensively before adequate fraud assessment was in place. In the year to April 2025, UK anti-fraud teams recovered a record £480 million in fraudulent payments, over a third of which related to pandemic-era schemes. This recovery underscored the need for a more proactive, prevention-led approach.

Developed by the PSFA Data Science team and powered by GPT-4.1, the Accelerator enables qualified fraud assessors to upload draft policy and scheme documentation and automatically generate a structured FRA covering potential fraud actors, actions, and outcomes. Critically, the tool analyses policy documents, not individual citizen data, positioning it as a policy design tool rather than a surveillance or targeting mechanism. By automating the research and initial drafting stages, it redirects specialist time towards review and validation. Human oversight is embedded throughout: all outputs are reviewed and enriched by qualified Fraud Subject Matter Experts before use, with automated PII detection and redaction built in.

Early testing indicates the tool could reduce fraud risk identification time by up to 80%, and it has already led to £480 million recovered in fraudulent payments in the year to April 2025, the highest single-year recovery by UK anti-fraud teams. Following Cabinet Office Technical Design Authority assurance in October 2025, the tool is entering public beta rollout across UK government, with international licensing underway for Five Eyes partner nations.

Lessons Learned
Prevention over recovery: integrating fraud controls at the policy design stage is significantly more cost-effective than pursuing recovery after exploitation has occurred.Human oversight is non-negotiable: qualified assessors validate and enrich every FRA before use, ensuring professional accountability throughout.Automate the routine, preserve the judgement: directing automation at research and drafting, rather than evaluative stages, maximises efficiency without compromising quality.Govern from the start: involving legal, ethics, and data privacy specialists from discovery through to rollout builds the trust necessary for responsible scaling.Overall, the Accelerator represents a deliberate shift from reactive recovery to proactive prevention, embedding fraud assessment earlier in the policy design process.

items.title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
items.category: Regulations, guidelines and standards
items.body:
A landmark UK Act of Parliament, which received Royal Assent in May 2024, that gives the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) new strategic market status (SMS) powers to regulate the most powerful digital platform companies and introduces a new pro-competition regime for digital markets.

The Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 is the primary legislative vehicle through which the UK government has sought to address concerns about market concentration in AI and digital platform markets. The DMCC Act creates the Digital Markets regime, administered by the CMA's Digital Markets Unit (DMU), which enables the CMA to designate specific large technology companies as having Strategic Market Status in a designated activity. SMS designation triggers a suite of obligations including conduct requirements (preventing self-preferencing, data access barriers and interoperability restrictions), pro-competitive interventions (structural or behavioural remedies), and enhanced merger scrutiny. The CMA has identified foundation model markets — including AI model APIs, AI-integrated search, and cloud infrastructure underpinning AI services — as priority areas for the Digital Markets regime. The CMA published its AI Foundation Models review in 2024, identifying concentration risks among a small number of US hyperscalers and AI labs. The DMCC Act also significantly strengthens consumer protection enforcement and streamlines merger review processes in a manner directly applicable to the wave of AI-related acquisitions and investments. SMS designation processes for the first cohort of technology companies began in 2025. Internationally, the DMCC approach is frequently compared with the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA).

items.title: British Business Bank (BBB) – SME Finance and AI Adoption Support
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
The UK Government's wholly-owned economic development bank, whose equity and debt programmes provide growth capital to innovative UK businesses including AI and technology firms, operating through accredited fund managers and lenders rather than lending directly.

Established in November 2014 and headquartered in Sheffield, the British Business Bank (BBB) is the UK's largest investor in venture and venture growth capital funds. It delivers its mandate through a suite of programmes: equity programmes (Enterprise Capital Funds, British Patient Capital, Long-term Investment for Technology and Science/LIFTS) and debt programmes (Growth Guarantee Scheme, ENABLE portfolio guarantees, Start Up Loans). BBB does not lend directly to most businesses; instead it provides funds and guarantees to accredited fund managers and lenders, crowding in private capital. As of June 2025, the BBB's total financial capacity was increased to GBP 25.6bn, enabling annual investments of approximately GBP 2.5bn and expected to crowd in tens of billions in private capital. In 2024/25, BBB supported GBP 6.8bn of finance for smaller businesses. A new GBP 4bn British Business Bank Industrial Strategy Growth Capital initiative will be deployed across eight growth-driving sectors including digital and technologies, advanced manufacturing, and life sciences, with AI identified as a key vertical. BBB explicitly supports direct early-stage investment into UK AI companies to help keep them in the UK longer term. The LIFTS initiative channelled a GBP 250m BBB commitment alongside GBP 250m from Phoenix Group into a Schroders Capital LTAF for UK science and technology scale-ups including AI companies. In March 2026, BBB committed GBP 50m as cornerstone investor in SuperSeed Fund III, focused on physical AI applications in manufacturing, energy, and construction. Target audience: UK SMEs and scale-ups, with a focus on underrepresented founders and regions outside London.

items.title: BDC Data to AI Program
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
A Business Development Bank of Canada programme providing Canadian SMEs with structured advisory services, personalised AI readiness diagnostics and roadmaps, cybersecurity assessments, and flexible term loan financing to adopt AI, automation, and cybersecurity solutions.

Launched on 4 December 2024 by BDC (Canada's bank for entrepreneurs, a federal Crown corporation), the Data to AI Program was developed in response to BDC research showing that only 39% of Canadian SME owners believed they were using AI, while 66% recognised AI tools when shown a list. The programme offers a structured four-stage approach: (1) Digital/AI diagnostic and readiness assessment; (2) Personalised advisory services to define business objectives and AI adoption roadmap; (3) Financing to cover the total cost of AI, automation, and cybersecurity integration — delivered as a term loan with a repayment period of up to eight years, covering consulting fees, software acquisition, and implementation costs; and (4) Connection to BDC's partner ecosystem for specialised services. The programme covers three technology pillars: AI solutions (understanding AI, adoption planning, and implementation); cybersecurity (assessment and safeguarding of digital assets); and digital automation (workflow process improvement). BDC committed CAD 500M in new financing capacity to support the programme alongside advisory services. The programme targets SMEs of all sizes across all sectors, particularly those in the early stages of digital and AI adoption. It builds on BDC's prior Digital Adoption Program and digital advisory capabilities.

items.title: Agent MIA (Argentine State's Artificial Intelligence Assistant)
items.original_name: MIA (Asistente de Inteligencia Artificial del Estado Argentino)
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.document_name: MIA (Asistente de Inteligencia Artificial del Estado Argentino)
items.body:
MIA is integrated into the national government's chatbot (TINA). It was conceived as a support agent for citizen services management based on information security, administrative transparency, and human oversight principles. It offers personalized responses according to each user's needs and context. It is based on LLAMA 4 (Meta) for speed, low operating cost, and open-source nature. Currently in its initial phase with two use cases: SMEs and Mi Argentina (citizens' platform).

The initiative seeks to address inefficiencies in public services by modernizing them to achieve a more transparent, efficient, and citizen-centered government. Specifically, it addresses the following points:
 It aims to reduce waiting times and simplify digital processes for citizens. It solves the problem of misinformation by drawing on a closed knowledge base that uses only official data, thus ensuring accuracy and avoiding bias.Unlike traditional chatbots that only respond, MIA can act: query data, generate reports, and perform administrative tasks under human supervision.MIA's main objectives focus on improving the interaction between the government and society: 
Supporting SMEs and assisting the 26 million users of the Mi Argentina app with their digital transactions.Offer a more agile, efficient, simple, and secure conversational experience.Save time for both users and government support teams.MIA is expected to evolve from a consultation assistant to a comprehensive government management tool: • We are working to expand the initiative and achieve integration into critical environments such as the Electronic Document Management System (GDE), Online Procedures (TAD), and the official portal Argentina.gob.ar. MIA has been designed to scale to a wide range of topics and services. In the next 12 to 18 months, the goal is for these AI agents to significantly simplify people's lives and make public administration more efficient at all levels. 

Currently, it already registers more than 1.5 million conversations per month. Impacts are measured using internal performance metrics for continuous improvement and the exploratory application of UNESCO's RAM Methodology. In the future, MIA will evolve from conversational to agentic, executing administrative tasks and generating reports in systems such as GDE and TAD. Over the next 12-18 months, it is expected to be the cornerstone for positioning Argentina as a regional AI hub, enabling a government that not only responds but also acts to simplify citizens' lives and optimize public administration.

items.title: AMALIA – Automatic Multimodal Language Assistant with Artificial Intelligence
items.original_name: AMALIA – Assistente Multimodal Automático de Linguagem com Inteligência Artificial
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.document_name: AMALIA – Assistente Multimodal Automático de Linguagem com Inteligência Artificial
items.body:
AMALIA is the first LLM designed for European Portuguese, with the aim of ensuring Portugal's linguistic and cultural sovereignty. The base version was launched in SEP25 and the full multimodal version (capable of interpreting text, images and video) arrives mid-2026. Use cases will focus on the areas of education, culture, speech, media, science and public administration. The model will be openly available so that it can be used and improved by scientists and development teams on any platform.

AMALIA is the first Large-Scale Language Model (LLM) designed specifically for European Portuguese language, using AI to process and generate natural language, with the ability to understand the linguistic diversity, cultural context, and historical references unique to Portugal. 

The main objective of AMALIA is to promote digital sovereignty, ensuring that sensitive national data can be processed securely and independently. It also aims to strengthen the national AI ecosystem by supporting innovation in key sectors such as education, culture, speech, media, science and public administration. 

AMALIA will be a multimodal model, capable of interpreting not only text but also speech, images and video, and its development implies an investment of €5,5 million, led by national research institutions and coordinated by the State Technological Reform Agency (ARTE). 

AMALIA shows strong performance in European Portuguese, outperforming other open models in lexicology and semantics. The base version is complete, and developed by over 60 researchers, reinforcing national digital sovereignty. Results are measured through technical benchmarking reports and evaluations in public services. Future impacts include broader use in education, public administration, and science, with the final version expected in mid-2026.

Key risks associated with AMALIA include establishing secure and compliant protocols for sharing non-public data, ensuring adequate funding and timely development of user interfaces for the defined use cases, and preventing data obsolescence. The critical conditions for the success of an initiative such as AMALIA include the effective productization of its use cases, ensuring that they move beyond prototypes into scalable, user-ready solutions, and the establishment of a robust inference infrastructure capable of supporting its widespread deployment across Public Administration.

All versions of the model, along with the training data, will be released as open source, making them freely available to researchers, public institutions, companies, and citizens. This initiative is the first major project under Portugal’s National Artificial Intelligence Agenda, reinforcing Portugal’s commitment to ethical, inclusive, and sovereign development. The current version is already available through the IAedu platform of the Foundation for Science and Technology (FCT), while the final version of AMALIA is expected to be launched in mid-2026.

items.title: AI for Growth
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
A CAD 174 million, three-year Canadian programme to accelerate domestic AI adoption by SMEs, delivered through Canada's National AI Institutes and Global Innovation Clusters.

AI for Growth is a targeted federal funding programme announced under Canada's 2025 Budget and operated by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED). It is delivered through Canada's three National AI Institutes — Amii (Alberta), Mila (Québec), and the Vector Institute (Ontario) — as well as the Global Innovation Clusters network. The programme has three primary objectives: to increase AI adoption among Canadian SMEs by connecting them with advisory support, tools, and funding; to accelerate the commercialisation of Canadian-developed AI research by facilitating pathways from lab to market; and to strengthen business capacity to adopt domestically developed AI technologies, thereby reducing reliance on foreign platforms. SMEs are the primary target beneficiary, with support encompassing access to compute resources, AI readiness assessments, structured adoption pathways, and skills development. The programme is designed to build on Canada's existing innovation infrastructure rather than create new parallel institutions, leveraging the established expertise and networks of the National AI Institutes.

items.title: AI Security Institute (formerly AI Safety Institute, AISI)
items.category: National – AI governance bodies or mechanisms
items.body:
The UK's national body for advanced AI safety and security research, model evaluation and international AI safety coordination. Originally established as the AI Safety Institute (AISI) in November 2023, it was renamed the AI Security Institute in January 2025 to reflect a broader mandate encompassing both safety and security risks from advanced AI systems.

The AI Security Institute was established following the Bletchley Park AI Safety Summit in November 2023, building directly on the Foundation Model Taskforce which had operated from April 2023. It was the first government-backed AI safety body in the world and served as the model for equivalent institutions subsequently established in the United States, Japan, Canada, France, South Korea and Singapore under the International Network of AI Safety Institutes (INAIS). In January 2025, the incoming Labour government renamed the Institute the AI Security Institute, broadening its mandate to encompass AI-enabled cybersecurity threats, offensive AI capabilities, and adversarial uses of AI systems alongside the original focus on frontier model safety evaluation. Core activities include: conducting pre-deployment and post-deployment evaluations of frontier AI models from developers including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Meta and others; publishing public-facing safety reports and evaluation methodologies; developing benchmarks and tooling for model assessment; contributing to international AI safety standards through INAIS, the OECD, ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42 and G7/G20 processes; and conducting research into systemic risks from advanced AI including misuse potential, deceptive alignment and emergent capabilities. The Institute operates the AI Safety Evaluations Platform (AISEP), an infrastructure enabling both UK government and invited international partners to run standardised model evaluations.

items.title: AI STRATEGIC WORKFORCE PLANNING
items.original_name: Στρατηγικό εργαλείο προγραμματισμού ανθρώπινου δυναμικού βασισμένου σε τεχνικές τεχνητής νοημοσύνης
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.document_name: Στρατηγικό εργαλείο προγραμματισμού ανθρώπινου δυναμικού βασισμένου σε τεχνικές τεχνητής νοημοσύνης
items.body:
The Ministry of the Interior is developing a digital workforce planning tool that supports decision-making based on big data and predictive technologies. The tool analyses demographic trends, retirements, skills and operational needs to produce 5–10 year staffing scenarios. It helps policymakers anticipate future needs, identify skill gaps, compare hiring and reskilling options, and better align staff with organisational goals.

The strategic workforce planning initiative aims to strengthen evidence‑based human resource management across public administration. It responds to long‑standing difficulties in anticipating staffing needs, managing demographic change, addressing skills mismatches and aligning workforce capacity with organisational priorities. By drawing on increasingly available HR, performance and administrative data, the initiative supports a shift from reactive staffing decisions toward forward‑looking workforce planning.

The initiative treats workforce planning as a strategic management function rather than an administrative task. It supports policymakers and managers in planning both the quantity and quality of the public‑sector workforce by identifying current and future staffing gaps, analysing skills requirements and assessing the impact of technological, demographic and economic change on roles and competencies. This approach strengthens alignment between organisational objectives and available skills over the medium to long term. To enable this, a dedicated digital workforce‑planning platform has been developed. The platform integrates demographic information, retirement trends, skills profiles and operational needs, and generates alternative staffing scenarios over a five‑ to ten‑year horizon. Users can compare different policy options, such as accelerated recruitment, internal mobility or targeted reskilling, making the platform a practical simulation tool for evidence‑based workforce‑strategy discussions.

Artificial intelligence and predictive analytics are used strictly as decision‑support tools. They analyse large datasets to identify patterns and forecast potential skills shortages, supporting structured assessment of hiring, mobility and reskilling options. All strategic and operational decisions remain under human responsibility. The initiative is aligned with broader HR digitalisation and performance‑management reforms, ensuring consistency with goal‑setting, evaluation and incentive frameworks. The platform has been developed and piloted in nine public entities, allowing real‑world testing of data integration, scenario generation and usability. Progress has been assessed through validation of data inputs, evaluation of scenario outputs and qualitative feedback from participating policymakers and managers. These pilots provided practical insights and supported refinement before wider deployment.

items.title: AI Research Resource (AIRR)
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
A government-led public AI compute capability (suite of AI-optimised supercomputers and gateways) to provide specialised compute to UK researchers, industry and SMEs for ambitious AI R&D.

AIRR is a partnership between the UK Government (DSIT), UKRI and multiple universities/technology partners that operates high-performance, AI-optimised systems (e.g., Isambard-AI, Dawn). It provides open access routes for academic and industry projects (including SME applicants), calls for compute allocations, researcher support and training. The UK Compute Roadmap commits major investment to expand AIRR capacity substantially by 2030, supporting both applied research and frontier AI work.

items.title: AI Growth Zones
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
AI Growth Zones are designated regions in the United Kingdom aimed at accelerating the development of AI infrastructure, including data centres and computing capacity, while fostering AI innovation ecosystems.

AI Growth Zones (AIGZs) are part of the UK government’s broader strategy to expand national AI capabilities and attract private investment in AI infrastructure. They are designed to host large-scale computing infrastructure such as AI data centres and high-performance computing facilities. The programme aims to accelerate AI development by streamlining planning procedures, ensuring reliable energy supply, and enabling faster deployment of data centre infrastructure. By concentrating infrastructure and expertise in designated areas, AIGZs aim to strengthen the UK’s AI ecosystem, improve access to advanced computing resources, and support both research and industrial AI development. The initiative also seeks to attract global AI investment while ensuring regional economic development.

items.title: AI Compute Access Fund
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
A federal programme that provides financial support and compute-credits to Canadian SMEs so they can access high-performance/cloud AI compute needed to train, test and deploy models for commercialisation.

Part of Canada’s Sovereign AI and compute strategy, this fund subsidises eligible compute costs (cloud & specialist AI infrastructure) for projects that demonstrate commercial potential. It supports projects with compute budgets typically ranging from six-figure amounts up to multi-million dollar projects, reduces the barrier to training larger models for SMEs, and is delivered through program calls and an application assessment process. The initiative aims to level the playing field between smaller Canadian firms and large cloud providers by subsidising compute costs and encouraging domestic AI capacity.

items.title: AI Bridging Cloud Infrastructure 3.0 (ABCI 3.0)
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
ABCI 3.0 is Japan's national AI computing infrastructure that provides access to supercomputing resources for developing sovereign AI capabilities. Operated by AIST and funded through Japan's METI, it delivers 6.2 exaflops of computing power using 6,128 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The infrastructure supports industry, academia, and government in developing large language models and advancing generative AI research, with priority given to national research institutes, universities, and startups.

ABCI 3.0 represents Japan's strategic response to growing global AI competition and the need for sovereign AI capabilities. As the third generation of ABCI infrastructure—first launched in August 2018—the system became fully operational in January 2025, providing unprecedented computing resources for AI development within Japan. In June 2025, ABCI 3.0 officially proved its status as Japan’s premier AI supercomputer by ranking 4th globally and 1st in Japan on the HPL-MxP benchmark, which measures mixed-precision AI computing performance. It also secured 15th place in the world (2nd in Japan) on the TOP500 list, reflecting its immense raw computational power.
The initiative addresses Japan's critical need to reduce dependence on foreign AI technologies while developing foundation models with deep understanding of Japanese language and culture. Built by Hewlett Packard Enterprise using NVIDIA's H200 Tensor Core GPUs connected via Quantum-2 InfiniBand networking, the system delivers peak performance of 6.22 exaflops in half precision and 3.0 exaflops in single precision—representing a 7 to 13 times improvement over the previous ABCI 2.0 system. As of May 2025, more than 60 R&D projects involving foundation models, LLMs, and multimodal AI were already active under its "Accelerated Use" program.
ABCI3.0 funded through METI's Economic Security Fund with an initial investment of ¥36 billion ($232 million). The infrastructure prioritizes resource allocation for public and strategic R&D purposes, particularly supporting national institutions, universities, and startups.
ABCI 3.0's mission has evolved from providing general AI infrastructure to focusing on cutting-edge challenges in sovereign AI development and supporting the domestic AI startup ecosystem. The system provides relaxed usage limits compared to previous versions, including increased node allocations and extended reserved durations, enabling larger-scale foundation model development. Looking ahead, ABCI 3.0 is a cornerstone for advancing "Physical AI"—integrating real-world data like 3D point clouds and sound into multimodal foundation models—marking the next frontier in Japan's strategy to enhance industrial competitiveness through sovereign AI technology.

items.title: AI Assist (IRAP)
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
A support programme helping SMEs adopt AI technologies (generative AI and deep learning) through advisory services and innovation support.

Delivered through the National Research Council Canada’s Industrial Research Assistance Program (IRAP), AI Assist pairs SMEs with Industrial Technology Advisors and approved third-party delivery organisations to carry out feasibility work, scoping, and tailored support for AI adoption (awareness, readiness assessment, pilot projects, ethical/responsible AI considerations). IRAP provides technical advice and can connect firms to funding streams or cost-share R&D activities. The programme focuses on practical SME uptake and helps firms progress from early experimentation to product-grade deployments.

items.title: UKRI AI Strategy
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
The UKRI AI Research and Innovation Strategic Framework is the first dedicated AI strategy for UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), the UK's largest public research funder.

Published in February 2026, the UKRI AI Strategy represents the organisation's biggest single targeted investment area for the spending period 2026–2030. It was developed in alignment with the UK Government's AI Opportunities Action Plan, the DSIT AI for Science Strategy (November 2025), and the UK's Industrial Strategy. The strategy sets out six priority action areas: (1) advancing core AI technologies; (2) transforming research through AI; (3) developing skills and talent; (4) accelerating innovation for economic growth; (5) championing responsible AI; and (6) building data and infrastructure capacity — including up to £250 million for cloud compute and £36 million to upgrade Cambridge's DAWN supercomputer. Key investments include up to £137 million for AI-enabled scientific discovery via DSIT's AI for Science Strategy. UKRI is uniquely positioned as the only public body investing across the entire value chain from skills and infrastructure to technology development, uniting universities, industry and government.

items.title: UK Sovereign AI Unit
items.category: National – AI governance bodies or mechanisms
items.body:
The UK Sovereign AI Unit is a government body established within the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) to build and harness the UK's domestic AI capabilities.

The Sovereign AI Unit was established in DSIT in 2025 as a core pillar of the UK AI Opportunities Action Plan. Chaired by venture capitalist James Wise (Balderton Capital), the Unit operates as a novel government fund structure designed to be the first choice for founders building essential parts of the UK's AI infrastructure. The Unit's mandate covers the full AI value chain: investing in compute infrastructure, supporting data assets, backing frontier model development, and enabling AI application companies. Key activities include launching open calls to researchers and companies through the AI Research Resource (AIRR), supporting 'Autonomous Labs' combining robotics and AI, and forging Memoranda of Understanding with leading AI firms such as Anthropic and OpenAI to advance responsible AI development aligned with UK values. The Unit works alongside the British Business Bank and UKRI, and collaborates with the UK Compute Roadmap to build a world-class compute ecosystem. It complements AI Growth Zones and the National Data Library as part of a broader national AI infrastructure strategy.

items.title: UK Health Data Research Service (HDRS)
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
The Health Data Research Service (HDRS) is a new UK-wide, government-owned company to transform how researchers and innovators access health and care data across the UK.

The HDRS was announced following the Sudlow Review ('Uniting the UK's Health Data: A Huge Opportunity for Society'), which identified the fragmented, slow and complex landscape for health data access as a critical barrier to research and innovation. At its core, the HDRS is built on a national network of Secure Data Environments (SDEs), expanding the existing NHS Research SDE Network. The HDRS will provide a 'single front door' through which researchers make standardised access requests, enabling them to access linked primary care, hospital, prescribing, mortality, genomic and diagnostic imaging data at national scale, while keeping data in secure environments and maintaining privacy through encryption, anonymisation and synthetic data techniques. The service has six stated goals: (1) providing secure access to linked national-scale health data; (2) leveraging major UK cohort studies and biobanks; (3) enabling access to diagnostic images, genomics and laboratory data for precision medicine; (4) supporting innovative data linkage; (5) streamlining governance; and (6) building public trust.

items.title: UK AI Skills Hub
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
A free national AI training programme targeting 10 million UK workers, with a specific goal of upskilling 2 million SME employees, delivered in partnership with 23 major technology companies.

The UK AI Skills Hub is a flagship component of the government's TechFirst initiative, launched in June 2025 and significantly expanded on 28 January 2026 (coinciding with the anniversary of the AI Opportunities Action Plan). The programme offers free AI training to all UK adults, delivered online through a government-backed platform developed in partnership with 23 major technology companies. Its stated ambition is to upskill 10 million workers by 2030, with 2 million of those targeted from the SME workforce. Courses range from foundational AI literacy modules (some under 20 minutes) suitable for non-technical staff, to professional-level qualifications for those in AI-adjacent roles. Completions are recognised through a government-backed AI Foundations digital badge, providing portable evidence of skills for employees and assurance for employers. The January 2026 expansion also introduced a £27 million TechLocal scheme to connect people with tech jobs in their local area, and a £7.8 million TechLocal AI Professional Degree and Traineeship Accelerator, which funds universities and colleges to develop new AI-focused higher education courses created with industry input.

items.title: UK AI Assurance Innovation Fund
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
The AI Assurance Innovation Fund is a £11 million initiative to support the development of innovative and novel AI assurance mechanisms.

The AI Assurance Innovation Fund was announced in September 2025 as part of DSIT's Trusted Third-Party AI Assurance Roadmap, which sets out the UK Government's vision for a credible and scalable AI assurance market. The fund is designed to address the challenge that transformative AI will present novel risks requiring continuous innovation in assurance methods and tools. It will issue £11 million to support research, pilot projects, prototypes and novel assurance methodologies, with a focus on scalable and adaptive solutions for highly capable AI systems. The fund is focused on the eight industrial strategy sectors and will work alongside the AI Security Institute's existing efforts on advanced AI security risks. DSIT will also explore opportunities for the fund to support the UK's AI Adoption Hubs by providing funding to pilot innovative assurance solutions alongside cutting-edge technologies. The initiative is part of a broader roadmap that also includes professionalisation efforts and skills development and information sharing guidelines.

items.title: BridgeAI (Innovate UK)
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
The Regional AI Adoption Hubs are part of the UK Government's effort to drive AI adoption beyond London and the South East, supporting businesses across the country with tailored, regional guidance, funding and expertise to implement AI in their operations.

The Regional AI Adoption Hubs form part of the UK's AI Opportunities Action Plan, which identified the geographic concentration of AI benefits as a key challenge. The hubs are designed to ensure AI-driven growth reaches all parts of the UK, particularly those with historically lower AI adoption. Delivered through Innovate UK's BridgeAI programme (launched April 2023, expanded at Autumn Budget 2025), the hubs are implemented in partnership with Digital Catapult, the Alan Turing Institute, the Hartree Centre, and the British Standards Institution. Their activities include: (1) connecting businesses with AI experts through innovation networks; (2) funding the development of new trusted AI services and technologies through co-creation between AI developers and end-users; (3) upskilling organisations through training programmes and the AI Skills Hub; and (4) providing access to AI adoption frameworks and scientific advice. The programme is structured around a series of open competitions and challenge calls, with grants typically ranging from GBP 25,000 to GBP 350,000 for SMEs and research organisations. The Technology Adoption Review 2025 reinforced the hub model as a key mechanism for sector-specific AI support. The hubs also feed into the broader AI Assurance Innovation Fund.

items.title: Albert API
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
Albert API is a shared AI service run by the French government to help public administrations use generative AI tools safely and easily. It gives ministries and public teams access to a selection of AI models through a single, secure interface, without each organisation having to build its own system. It was developed to avoid duplication, reduce costs, and speed up the deployment of useful AI services for public officials.

Albert API is a shared, government-run AI service that provides French public administrations with secure access to a range of generative AI models through a single interface. It is designed to support ministries and public sector teams in building AI-enabled features into their tools and services, without each organisation having to deploy and operate its own AI infrastructure. By offering a common technical foundation, Albert API helps accelerate adoption while keeping control, security, and cost management at the centre of the approach.

The initiative responds to a growing challenge across government: AI projects have often developed in parallel, leading to duplicated investments, fragmented technical choices, and uneven levels of maturity. At the same time, the computing resources required to run modern AI models are expensive and difficult to scale responsibly. Albert API addresses this by pooling resources and expertise, offering a standard way to access models and monitor usage, and making it easier for administrations to move from experimentation to reliable deployment.

Albert API is a key component of the broader interministerial strategy for generative AI, alongside complementary services such as document analysis, transcription, and retrieval from trusted information sources. Its objectives are to reduce barriers to entry for public teams, improve the consistency and safety of deployments, and enable faster delivery of practical use cases for public officials (such as drafting support, summarisation, and information search). It also supports stronger governance through usage tracking and cost controls, helping administrations scale AI in a transparent and accountable way.

Over time, Albert API has evolved from an initial shared inference service into a more structured foundation for interministerial AI deployment. It is expected to continue expanding in coverage and capabilities, while remaining interoperable and adaptable to different ministerial needs. For example, LaSuite Numerique integrates with Albert API to provide AI functionalities within several of its applications, including Visio (videoconferencing), Docs (collaborative document editing) and Grist (online spreadsheet and data management)This gradual scaling approach supports broader institutionalisation of AI across government, ensuring that new uses can grow on top of a stable, secure, and shared base rather than being rebuilt repeatedly across organisations.

items.title: APS AI Plan - Artificial Intelligence (AI) Plan for the Australian Public Service (APS)
items.category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
items.body:
The AI Plan for the Australian Public Service (APS) will improve government service delivery, policy outcomes, efficiency, and productivity, through substantially increasing the use of AI in government. Every public servant will have the training and guidance required to use generative AI safely and responsibly, alongside secure access to generative AI tools, and every agency will have a Chief AI Officer to drive adoption, with AI use tracked and reported on.

The Australian Government is focused on capturing the opportunity of AI and, to ensure the benefits of this technology are shared equitably, creating a higher standard of living for all Australians. The APS AI Plan positions the government to improve service delivery, policy outcomes, efficiency and productivity by substantially increasing the safe and responsible use of AI in government. The APS AI Plan is built around three core pillars that work together to enable the safe, effective and scalable use of artificial intelligence across the Australian Public Service.
Trust Pillar. Focuses on ensuring AI is used safely, ethically and transparently. It builds on existing security and privacy safeguard governing the use of ICT and data and strengthens governance and improves transparency to maintain public trust, manage risk, and ensure AI use aligns with APS values and community expectations.People Pillar. Focuses on building capability and supporting the public service workforce by ensuring ensures public servants are equipped with the right skills to use AI responsibly and effectively. This includes access to training, consultation and engagement, and other support to use AI confidently and responsibly, recognising the impact of AI on roles, skills and ways of working.Tools Pillar. Focuses on empowering the public service workforce through access to secure, fit for purpose AI technologies. It supports the rollout of shared platforms and tools that enable efficient adoption of AI, collaboration across government, and reuse of solutions where possible.APS AI Plan Objectives:
Improving AI literacy. As AI becomes increasingly widespread and available, everyone in government needs basic AI literacy and training. Leading by example. The government has an important role to play in modelling responsible and ethical AI adoption. Expanding generative AI use. Current levels of AI adoption are inconsistent.
